18B. Results

i. Phenology

Entire period: 1981–2025
Over 1981–2025, predicted adult emergence and egg hatch showed mixed regional trends, with later events common across portions of the northern and central United States and earlier events in other regions (Figure 1, Figure 2). Significant changes were concentrated in scattered areas of the central and eastern United States.








Figure 1: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first adult emergence for TABS across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.













Figure 2: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first egg hatch for TABS across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.







Recent period: 2001–2025
During 2001–2025, later predicted adult emergence and egg hatch were prominent across portions of the northern and central United States, while earlier events occurred in scattered western and southern regions (Figure 3, Figure 4). Significant changes were relatively limited but included localized areas in the central United States.








Figure 3: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first adult emergence for TABS across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.













Figure 4: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first egg hatch for TABS across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.








ii. Climatic suitability

Entire period: 1981–2025
Predicted cold stress decreased broadly across the northern United States over 1981–2025, while heat stress increased across the western and southern United States (Figure 5, Figure 6). Significant increases in climatic suitability were concentrated in portions of the southern and central United States, with additional localized areas along the Pacific Coast (Figure 7).








Figure 5: Changes (units/year) in predicted cold stress for TABS across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.

Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 7: Changes in predicted climatic suitability for TABS across the CONUS over the 44-year period (1981–2025). Suitability is defined as areas not excluded by climate stress. Positive changes (warmer colors) indicate an increased likelihood of establishment, whereas negative changes (cooler colors) indicate a decreased likelihood of establishment.







Recent period: 2001–2025
During 2001–2025, increases in predicted cold stress became more apparent across portions of the northern and central interior, while heat stress continued to increase across the Southwest and southern Great Plains (Figure 8, Figure 9). Climatic-suitability increases remained localized, particularly in the southern and central United States (Figure 10).

Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 10: Changes in predicted climatic suitability for TABS across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Suitability is defined as areas not excluded by climate stress. Positive changes (warmer colors) indicate an increased likelihood of establishment, whereas negative changes (cooler colors) indicate a decreased likelihood of establishment.

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
18C. Discussion
The TABS results show substantial regional variation in predicted phenological change, with the recent period characterized by later adult emergence and egg hatch in portions of the northern and central United States. In environmentally suitable regions, shifts in phenology could affect the timing and number of generations because TABS is multivoltine and its development is strongly temperature dependent. The maps therefore suggest that surveillance and management timing may need to account for regional differences in seasonal development.
The increase in predicted climatic suitability across portions of the southern and central United States is consistent with the species’ modeled preference for warmer conditions and the long-term reduction in cold stress. At the same time, increasing heat stress in the Southwest could limit suitability in the warmest areas. The more localized recent-period suitability changes suggest that establishment risk has not increased uniformly across the CONUS.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

17A. Introduction
The Sunn pest (SUNP), Eurygaster integriceps Puton, 1881 (Hemiptera: Scutelleridae), is a serious and economically important pest of wheat, barley, oats, rye, and sorghum. Its geographic range spans latitudes 25° to 55° N across Eurasia, including much of Eastern Europe, West Asia, Central Asia, and North Africa (Paulian and Popov 1980, Critchley 1998, Mackesy and Moylett 2018, EPPO 2021). Both larvae and adults damage host plants by causing plant death, arresting grain development, or degrading the gluten content of surviving wheat kernels (Paulian and Popov 1980, Critchley 1998). As a result, flour produced from infested grain yields bread of poor quality and reduced digestibility (Paulian and Popov 1980). In the absence of effective control measures, infestations can lead to complete crop loss (Kivan and Kilic 2005). If introduced to the United States, SUNP could cause substantial economic damage to wheat and barley production, which were valued at $7.9 billion and $685 million, respectively, in 2017 (USDA-NASS 2019). Areas at most risk for establishment of SUNP based on host presence are in the Midwestern United States, the Columbia River valley, and the lower Mississippi River valley (Macksey and Moylett 2018).
SUNP is a univoltine pest with two major periods in its annual life cycle (Davari and Parker 2018). Adults spend late summer through winter in aestivation and overwintering sites, where they undergo obligatory diapause and remain largely inactive until spring temperatures reach approximately 10–14 °C, triggering emergence and migration to cereal fields for reproduction (Banks et al. 1961, Critchley 1998, Parker et al. 2011, Islamoglu 2022). Following development through five nymphal instars and the subsequent adult emergence, adults migrate approximately 10–20 km to hillside aestivation and overwintering sites, which occur at higher elevations under bushes in the southern part of the range and in deciduous Quercus forests in the northern part (Paulian and Popov 1980, Critchley 1998, Davari and Parker 2018). This seasonal movement between agricultural and non-crop habitats complicates management and requires appropriately timed monitoring and control (Critchley 1998, Davari and Parker 2018), while regional geographic features that influence temperature can affect the timing and direction of migration (Parker et al. 2011, Islamoglu 2022). Potentially suitable environmental conditions for SUNP occur across most of the contiguous United States (CONUS), although mountainous and higher-latitude regions of the West may be unsuitable for development because of insufficient thermal accumulation (Aljaryian et al. 2016, Barker and Coop 2020). Nevertheless, the species’ migratory behavior could allow adults to move between suitable cereal-growing areas and nearby seasonal aestivation or overwintering sites, potentially facilitating persistence where seasonal conditions limit activity.
A model for SUNP developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the CONUS at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 12.2 °C and upper threshold of 36 °C for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the adults is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of −30 °C and 40 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for SUNP, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-sunp-parameters. Details on model parameterization are available at USPest.org (Barker and Coop 2020).

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
17C. Discussion
The SUNP maps indicate earlier phenological timing over much of the CONUS during the full period, but a weaker and more heterogeneous pattern during the recent period. Because SUNP development and seasonal movement are closely associated with temperature and seasonal conditions, these shifts could alter the timing of movement and activity in regions where the species can establish.
The long-term increase in predicted suitability across portions of the northern Plains and Great Lakes is consistent with declining cold stress in those regions. Recent increases in cold stress across parts of the same broad region correspond with fewer significant suitability changes, suggesting that the establishment signal has become less consistent during the recent period.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
16A. Introduction
The small tomato borer (STB), Neoleucinodes elegantalis (Guenée) (Lepidoptera: Pyralidae), is an oligophagous pest of Solanum species, including tomato, eggplant, red and green pepper, lulo (naranjilla), and wild Solanum spp. (Molet 2012, OEPP/EPPO 2015). Native to South America, it has expanded its range into Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean (Molet 2012, OEPP/EPPO 2015, Díaz-Montilla 2013a). The species occupies a wide range of climatic conditions in South America, although its distribution varies depending on host plant availability and altitude (Díaz Montilla 2013b). Larvae develop through five instars, with the third through fifth instars responsible for the majority of fruit damage, and development rates that may vary by host plant (Serrano Plaza et al. 1992, Díaz-Montilla 2013a). Infestations can result in severe economic losses, with reported yield reductions in South American tomato crops ranging from 45% to 90% (Díaz Montilla and Kondo 2024). If introduced to the United States, regions with high levels of tomato and pepper production would be particularly vulnerable (Molet 2012, USDA-APHIS-PPQ 2024). In addition, STB poses a significant barrier to the export of solanaceous crops from South America to the United States and the European Union (Díaz-Montilla 2013a, Díaz-Montilla 2013b). The pest has been intercepted hundreds of times at United States ports of entry, with most interceptions originating from Brazil (Molet 2012).
Potentially suitable environmental conditions for STB occur in western portions of the Pacific states, the Southeast, and parts of the southern Northeast, although colder conditions limit suitability across much of the northern United States (Barker et al. 2020). In its native range, increases in temperature and precipitation appear to favor STB populations, while arid conditions can limit its distribution, suggesting that moisture availability may influence STB distribution and climatic suitability in the contiguous United States (CONUS; Silva et al. 2020, da Silva et al. 2018). Annual voltinism also varies substantially with climate, with models predicting 2–11 generations per year in Colombia and 5–10 generations in Brazil (de Moraes and Foerster 2015, dos Santos and Marchioro 2021). STB does not appear to have a diapause or distinct overwintering stage and can produce continuous, overlapping generations, with voltinism generally increasing toward warmer, lower-latitude regions (Serrano Plaza et al. 1992, Moraes and Foerster 2015, Barker et al. 2020). In CONUS, annual voltinism is predicted to range from one to two generations in colder parts of the Pacific Northwest to seven to nine generations in coastal areas of the Southeast, with three to six generations across much of the remainder of the CONUS (Barker et al. 2020).
A model for tomato fruit borer developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the CONUS at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 8.89 °C and upper threshold of 30 °C for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the adult is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of 6 °C and 32 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for tomato fruit borer, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-stb-parameters. Details on model parameterization are available at USPest.org (Barker et al. 2020).

16B. Results

i. Phenology

Entire period: 1981–2025
Over 1981–2025, predicted adult emergence and egg hatch generally occurred earlier across much of the southern and eastern United States, while later events were evident across portions of the northern and western interior (Figure 1, Figure 2). During 2001–2025, adult emergence and egg hatch showed a stronger tendency toward later dates across portions of the northern and central United States, with earlier events remaining in scattered western and southern areas (Figure 3, Figure 4). text:
16C. Discussion
The STB results show a clear difference between the long-term and recent phenological patterns. Earlier emergence and egg hatch were common over 1981–2025, whereas later events became more prominent in the recent period across portions of the northern and central United States. This contrast suggests that recent regional climate variability has substantially influenced the short-term phenological signal and should be considered when interpreting current management timing.
The increase in predicted suitability across northern and central regions over the full period coincided with declining cold stress, suggesting that warming has reduced a temperature-related limitation in those areas. The recent increase in cold stress and corresponding reduction in suitability changes indicate that this long-term expansion signal is less evident during 2001–2025.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

text:
15A. Introduction
Widespread across Europe, northern Africa, and Asia, the silver Y moth (SLYM), Autographa gamma Linnaeus (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae), is a highly polyphagous defoliator of cereals, Brassica spp., legumes, tobacco, and a wide range of fruit and vegetable crops, with particularly significant impacts on sugar beet (Maceljski and Balarin 1972, Venette et al. 2003, Sullivan and Molet 2007, EPPO 2019, Carneiro 2022). Adults undertake annual migrations to northern breeding regions across Eurasia to avoid the hot, dry conditions of Mediterranean overwintering areas (Honěk et al. 2002, Chapman et al. 2012, Chapman et al. 2015, Saulich et al. 2017, Becher and Revadi 2020). Population outbreaks in these breeding regions occur sporadically and are often associated with periods of unusually wet weather (Maceljski and Balarin 1974, Carneiro 2022). The species is considered a high-risk invasive agricultural pest for the United States, with the potential to damage more than 200 plant species, including lettuce, cabbage, and grape (Sullivan and Molet 2014). It has been intercepted hundreds of times at United States ports of entry on approximately 130 plant taxa and is considered to have a high likelihood of establishment if introduced (Sullivan and Molet 2014).
Potentially suitable environmental conditions for SLYM occur across much of the United States, although winter conditions may prevent long-term persistence across much of the northern United States, where annual migration from southern source populations could allow temporary establishment during the growing season (Barker and Coop 2020, PPQ 2025). In Eurasia, populations generally complete one to four generations per year, with voltinism increasing toward lower latitudes (Saulich et al. 2017, Carneiro 2022). Similarly, SLYM is predicted to complete one to five generations annually in the contiguous United States (CONUS), with the highest voltinism occurring in the Southeast, Southwest, and California (Barker and Coop 2020, PPQ 2025). Hot, dry conditions may also limit populations, with increased drying in the Mediterranean region potentially reducing northward migration and consequently affecting annual population size and generation number (Ellis 2016).
A model for SLYM developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the CONUS at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 8.9 ºC and upper threshold of 35.0 ºC for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the larva is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of −1 °C and 38 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for SLYM, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-slym-parameters. Details on model parameterization are available at USPest.org (Barker and Coop 2020).

15C. Discussion
Predicted phenology for SLYM showed regional changes in timing but relatively limited changes in climatic suitability. Earlier events in portions of the West and central United States could shift seasonal activity, while contrasting trends in northern and eastern areas indicate that the response is geographically heterogeneous. The recent-period maps also show that shorter-term climate patterns can differ from the longer-term signal.
The broad decline in cold stress over the full period did not produce a corresponding broad increase in predicted climatic suitability. This suggests that SLYM is not strongly constrained by the modeled cold-stress threshold across most of the CONUS. Increasing heat stress in the Southwest likewise produced little measurable change in overall suitability.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
14A. Introduction
The common or cotton cutworm (SLI), Spodoptera litura (Fabricius, 1775) (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae), is a highly polyphagous pest that feeds on at least 120 plant species, including economically important crops such as corn, cotton, groundnut, potato, soybean, sweet potato, tea, tobacco, and a wide range of vegetables (Venette et al. 2003, Sullivan 2007, Bragard et al. 2019, EPPO 2023). Females lay eggs on host plants, and within a few days, emerging larvae begin feeding on plant tissue, causing extensive damage that can lead to stunted growth and reduced marketability (Sullivan 2007). Native to Southeast Asia, SLI is now distributed across Australia, Oceania, several African islands, Hawaii, and other regions of Asia (Bragard et al. 2019, EPPO 2023). The pest has been present in Hawaii since 1964 and has been intercepted hundreds of times at United States ports of entry, primarily through cargo and passenger baggage (Venette et al. 2003, Sullivan 2007). The species has developed resistance to numerous insecticides and transgenic Bt cotton and is capable of long-distance migration, potentially aided by typhoons (Tu et al. 2010, Fu et al. 2015, Wan et al. 2008, Bragard et al. 2019, Murata et al. 1998). Severe defoliation caused by larval feeding has led to significant crop damage and economic losses in affected regions (Murata et al. 1998, Prasad et al. 2013, Bragard et al. 2019, Maharjan et al. 2023).
Potentially environmentally suitable areas for establishment for SLI in the contiguous United States (CONUS) include much of the southeastern United States and along the Pacific Coast (Coop 2018). If introduced to the United States, SLI could potentially overwinter in protected environments such as greenhouses or establish northern migratory populations (Bragard et al. 2019). Development and fecundity are strongly influenced by temperature, humidity, and host plant quality (Garad et al. 1985, EPPO 2023, Maharjan et al. 2023, Fu et al. 2025). SLI does not undergo diapause and therefore cannot survive winter conditions in areas north of approximately 30°N in China, where it instead establishes seasonal migratory populations (Fand et al. 2015, Fu et al. 2015, Bragard et al. 2019, EPPO 2023). SLI completes 3-12 generations in tropical regions versus three generations in colder parts of its distribution, including northern China (EPPO 2023). Consistent with its high reproductive potential under warm conditions, a DDRP model predicted one to ten possible generations annually in the conterminous United States, with four to six generations predicted across much of the Southeast and California (Coop 2018). SLI may also respond to changing temperatures through shifts in its geographic distribution and population growth, although warming could reduce suitability in some areas if temperatures exceed optimal conditions for development (Fand et al. 2015, Fu et al. 2025).
A model for SLI was developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the CONUS at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 10.6 ºC and upper threshold of 40 ºC for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the pupa is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of −3 °C and 44 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for SLI, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-sli-parameters. Details on model parameterization are available at USPest.org (Coop 2018).

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
14C. Discussion
The SLI maps indicate that phenological trends vary by event and region, with no single directional pattern dominating the CONUS. This variability suggests that changes in one developmental event should not necessarily be assumed to represent changes in all stages. Where significant phenological shifts occur, monitoring and management schedules may need to be adjusted regionally.
Despite substantial long-term declines in predicted cold stress across northern regions, the climatic-suitability maps showed little significant change. The limited heat-stress signal further suggests that climatic conditions remain broadly within the modeled suitability range across most of the CONUS, at least with respect to the stress thresholds represented by the model.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
13A. Introduction
The spotted lanternfly (SLF), Lycorma delicatula (White) (Hemiptera: Fulgoridae), is a highly polyphagous planthopper that feeds on a broad range of agricultural and non-agricultural plants, including grapevines, fruit and nut trees, and ornamental species (Chu 1930, Barringer and Ciafré 2020, EPPO 2025). Adults cause direct damage by feeding on plant sap, while the accumulation of honeydew promotes the growth of sooty mold, which can inhibit photosynthesis and attract additional pests (Dara et al. 2015, Urban and Leach 2023). Native to China, SLF was first detected in the United States in 2014 in Pennsylvania and has since spread to at least 20 eastern states (Urban and Leach 2023, NYSIPM 2025). The widespread presence of its preferred host, tree-of-heaven [Ailanthus altissima (Mill.) Swingle], has facilitated its rapid expansion (Barringer and Ciafré 2020). In suburban and urban environments, SLF can become a significant nuisance, with large aggregations of adults often swarming on trees (Urban and Leach 2023). The species has already caused substantial economic impacts, including estimated annual losses of $8.8 million to New York’s grape industry alone (Pinto et al. 2025).
Modeling studies indicate that SLF has not yet filled its fundamental niche in the contiguous United States (CONUS) under current weather patterns, with suitable conditions extending across much of the Pacific Coast and eastern United States (Jones et al. 2022, Wakie et al. 2019, Barker et al. 2025). The coldest regions of the CONUS, particularly portions of the Midwest and Northeast, may be less suitable for establishment (Wakie et al. 2019, Barker et al. 2025), although urban heat island effects could facilitate establishment in colder areas beyond the currently predicted range (Owen et al. 2024). SLF phenology may also shift in response to changing weather patterns. Analysis of citizen science observations from 2014 to 2022 found earlier adult emergence and later winter die-off as SLF expanded its range in the eastern United States (Owen et al. 2024). However, the effects of temperature, photoperiod, and other environmental factors on egg diapause and developmental rates remain incompletely understood, limiting predictions of how SLF may respond to changing weather patterns (Keena and Nielsen 2021, Calvin et al. 2023). Diapause may buffer populations against weather variability by enhancing overwintering egg survival and accelerating development and fecundity during summer and fall heat waves (Lewkiewicz et al. 2024). SLF is currently considered univoltine, including in warmer regions of China, and whether it can complete multiple generations annually in warmer areas of the United States remains uncertain (Keena and Nielsen 2021, Calvin et al. 2023).
A model for spotted lanternfly developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the CONUS at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 10 °C and upper threshold of 35 °C for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the egg is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of −16 °C and 37 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for spotted lanternfly, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-slf-parameters. Details on model parameterization are available at USPest.org (Barker et al. 2025).

text:
13C. Discussion
The SLF maps show a mixed phenological response, with the direction of change varying geographically and between the two periods. The absence of a single dominant spatial direction suggests that the timing of SLF development may respond differently to regional climate trends. Because the species is already capable of substantial spread in North America, localized changes in predicted phenology may be particularly relevant for surveillance timing in newly suitable areas.
Although cold and heat stress changed across broad areas, relatively little of that variation translated into significant changes in predicted climatic suitability. The long-term reduction in cold stress across northern regions could reduce one climatic constraint on establishment, but recent increases in cold stress in portions of the northern interior may have moderated this trend.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
12A. Introduction
The pine-tree lappet moth, Dendrolimus pini Linnaeus (Lepidoptera: Lasiocampidae) (PTLM), is an economically important pest of pine trees that is native to Europe and Asia (Hardin and Suazo 2012). Its current range includes Europe, Russia, Kazakhstan, Northern China, and Morocco (Hardin and Suazo 2012, EPPO 2024). PTLM’s primary host is the Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris), but it can successfully develop on 17 other species of pine, Douglas fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii), and Eastern hemlock (Tsuga canadensis), and may be able to successfully develop on Pinus spp. outside of its current range (Hardin and Suazo 2012, Łukowski 2021). Surviving affected trees take several years to recover from defoliation and are more susceptible to other forest pests (Hardin and Suazo 2012). If introduced to the United States, PTLM could cause significant damage to forests dominated by pine and monoculture pin plantations, potentially resulting in economic damage to the timber and Christmas tree industries (Hardin and Suazo 2012, Ray et al. 2016).
Climate suitability models indicate that PTLM could establish across much of the contiguous United States, although predictions vary among models, with the most suitable areas generally concentrated in temperate forest regions of the Northeast, Midwest, Appalachia, and Pacific Northwest (Barker and Coop 2020, Hardin and Suazo 2012). In Europe, the species is typically univoltine but may require two or more years to complete its life cycle in cooler regions (Moore and Evans 2016, Sukovata 2019). DDRP predicts one generation per year across much of the western and northern United States, two generations in parts of Appalachia and the Midwest, and three to four generations in portions of the Southeast (Barker and Coop 2020). Host species can affect larval and pupal development rates, and photoperiod regulates diapause and subsequent spring emergence (Hardin and Suazo 2012, Winokur 1991, Łukowski 2021). PTLM outbreaks have also been associated with warmer and drier conditions, which may influence pest development directly or indirectly through effects on the host plant (Lesniak 1976, Hardin and Suazo 2012, Moore and Evans 2016, Hentschel et al. 2018).
A model for PTLM developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 7.2 ºC and upper threshold of 30.0 ºC for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the larva is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of −15 °C and 30 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for PTLM, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-ptlm-parameters. Details on model parameterization are Online at USPest.org (Barker and Coop 2020).

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
12C. Discussion
Predicted phenology for PTLM was more spatially heterogeneous than for several of the other species, particularly during the recent period. Earlier egg hatch across broad areas could shift the timing of early-season activity, whereas the contrasting adult-emergence patterns indicate that different stages may respond differently to regional climate trends. Management timing may therefore benefit from considering multiple phenological events rather than relying on a single event.
The full-period increase in predicted suitability across portions of the central and eastern United States coincided with widespread decreases in cold stress and increasing heat stress in warmer regions. The recent-period increase in cold stress across parts of the northern interior may help explain the reduced spatial extent of suitability changes during 2001–2025.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

11A. Introduction
The Old World bollworm (OWBW), Helicoverpa armigera (Hübner) (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae), is a highly polyphagous pest that feeds on agricultural crops from 68 plant families, including chickpea, corn, cotton, tobacco, tomato, potato, and soybean (Cunningham and Zalucki 2014, EPPO 2020). Larvae are the primary damaging life stage of OWBW, as feeding by larvae directly damages vegetative and reproductive plant tissues and can cause substantial yield loss (Rogers and Brier 2010, Cameron et al. 2001). It is widely distributed across much of Europe, Asia, Africa, and Australasia, and began expanding into Central and South America in 2013 (EPPO 2025). In 2015, several specimens were detected in Florida, although populations did not become established (Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services 2015). The species is capable of long-distance migration, traveling up to 2,000 km when assisted by favorable winds (Widmer and Schofield 1983). It has also developed resistance to multiple insecticides and some transgenic crops (EFSA 2014). If established in the United States, OWBW could place crops valued at an estimated $78 billion annually at risk of damage (Kriticos et al. 2015).
Environmental suitability for OWBW is widespread across the United States, with modeling studies predicting suitable conditions across much of the eastern United States and portions of the West (Kriticos et al. 2015, Coop 2018). In the United States, the number of generations per year varies geographically, with up to 10 generations predicted in Florida, while generation numbers are lower in more temperate regions (Coop 2018). Under favorable conditions, generations can be completed in approximately 30 days, and up to 12 generations per year have been reported in tropical regions (EPPO 2020). OWBW is highly fecund, with females producing up to 3,000–4,000 eggs and eggs hatching in as little as three days under optimal conditions (Hardwick 1965, Silva et al. 2018). The species can enter facultative diapause in response to temperature and photoperiod, with diapause incidence increasing with latitude, short-day photoperiods at 20 °C can induce diapause during the early fifth instar, although low temperatures may also induce diapause independently of photoperiod under appropriate conditions (Hackett and Gatehouse 1982, Nibouche 1998, Kurban et al. 2005, Mironidis and Savopoulou-Soultani 2012, Shimizu et al. 2006). Development and population dynamics may also vary among host plant species (Liu et al. 2004, Silva et al. 2018).
A model for OWBW developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 10.6 ºC and upper threshold of 38 ºC for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the pupa is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of −4 °C and 39 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for OWBW, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-owbw-parameters. Details on model parameterization are Online at USPest.org (Coop 2018).

The OWBW maps indicate widespread regional changes in phenological timing, with earlier adult emergence and egg hatch occurring across many portions of the CONUS over the full period. The decline in cold stress across northern regions and corresponding increases in climatic suitability suggest a potential reduction in cold limitation over the long term. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
10A. Introduction
The oak ambrosia beetle (OAB), Platypus quercivorus Murayama (Coleoptera: Platypodidae), is a destructive forest pest distributed across India, Indonesia, Japan, and Papua New Guinea (Davis et al. 2005; USDA-APHIS 2011; EPPO 2020). The beetle vectors its symbiotic fungal pathogen, Raffaelea quercivora Kubono & Shin-Ito, which causes Japanese oak wilt disease (JOW) by disrupting tracheary function and can kill both healthy and stressed trees (Kubono and Ito 2002; Kamata et al. 2002; Davis et al. 2005; Kobayashi and Ueda 2005). Suitable host plants for reproduction include species of Quercus as well as other members of the Fagaceae, including chestnut (Castanea spp.), chinquapin (Castanopsis spp.), and stone oaks (Lithocarpus spp.), although OAB may also attack non-host tree species near areas experiencing mass infestation (Davis et al. 2005). The beetle–fungus complex has caused extensive oak mortality in Japan, where OAB preferentially attacks larger trees with higher water content, making abandoned oak coppice forests particularly vulnerable to infestation (Kobayashi and Ueda 2005; Nakajima 2019; EPPO 2020). If introduced to the United States, OAB and JOW could pose substantial economic, environmental, and social risks because of the potential for mortality of susceptible oak and other Fagaceae species. Although R. quercivora has only been reported from Japan, the distribution of OAB across multiple countries in Asia and Oceania highlights the potential for movement of the beetle through international trade and other pathways (Davis et al. 2005; USDA-APHIS 2011; EPPO 2020).
Several studies have predicted suitable conditions for OAB across much of the United States, although the predicted range varies among studies (USDA-APHIS 2011; Barker and Coop 2020; Takeuchi et al. 2023). Suitable conditions have been predicted across most of the country, including much of the Pacific Coast, Puerto Rico, and Hawaii, with the northern Midwest generally representing areas of lower suitability (USDA-APHIS 2011; Barker and Coop 2020; Takeuchi et al. 2023). Areas with abundant oak resources would therefore be expected to face the greatest risk of establishment and impact. OAB could potentially complete one to three generations annually in the United States, compared with generally one generation per year in Japan, although a second generation may occasionally occur (Kamata et al. 2002; Barker and Coop 2020; Takeuchi et al. 2023). When development is incomplete before winter, larvae overwinter as fifth instars (Kinuura 1995, Kinuura 2002, USDA-APHIS 2011). OAB is also capable of active flight and exhibits greater flight activity under humid conditions, while warmer temperatures during the rainy season may further increase dispersal activity (EPPO 2020; Kobayashi 2020).
A model for OAB developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 11.1 ºC and upper threshold of 38 ºC for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the larva is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of −10 °C and 38 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for OAB, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-oab-parameters. Details on model parameterization are available at USPest.org (Barker and Coop 2020).

9A. Introduction
Native to Australia, the light brown apple moth (LBAM), Epiphyas postvittana (Walker) (Lepidoptera: Tortricidae), is an invasive species established in the United States, the United Kingdom, New Zealand, New Caledonia, and the Azores, with additional interceptions reported worldwide (Danthanarayana 1975, EPPO 2024). This highly polyphagous pest has a host range exceeding 500 plant species, although its most significant economic impacts have been observed in apples, pears, and grapes (Brockerhoff et al. 2011). Infestations can create market access challenges due to the risk of transporting live larvae on a wide variety of host plants (Suckling and Brockerhoff 2010). In the United States, its distribution is currently limited to Hawaii, where it was first reported in 1893, and California, where it was confirmed in 2007 and now persists primarily in the San Francisco Bay Area, the Central Coast, and parts of southern California (Zimmerman 1978; Suckling and Brockerhoff 2010; Barker et al. 2020).
Previous modeling studies indicated suitable environmental conditions for LBAM across much of the southeastern United States and along the Pacific coast (Lozier & Mills 2011, He et al. 2012, Barker et al. 2020). Because LBAM does not undergo winter diapause, its distribution and population persistence are likely constrained in colder regions by minimum winter temperatures (Bürgi and Mills 2010). Cold tolerance varies among larval instars, with reported lower lethal temperatures ranging from –10.5 °C to –0.9 °C (Bürgi and Mills 2010), and associations with certain host plants may further increase larval cold tolerance and overwintering survival (Morey et al. 2016). In warmer regions, the absence of diapause or other strong seasonal synchronizing cues, such as photoperiod or temperature, allows LBAM to maintain overlapping generations throughout the year (Buergi et al. 2011). Consistent with this life-history strategy, the DDRP model predicted as many as nine generations per year in portions of the contiguous United States in 2018, although field observations in California reported an average of 3.27 generations in San Francisco and 4.58 generations in Santa Cruz (Buergi et al. 2011, Barker et al. 2020). Beyond temperature, population growth may also be influenced by rainfall and relative humidity, with higher growth rates reported under cooler temperatures and moderate moisture conditions (Danthanarayana 1995). Together, these findings indicate that LBAM risk is influenced by multiple interacting environmental factors, including winter temperature, temperature during the growing season, and moisture conditions.
A model for LBAM developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 7.2 °C and upper threshold of 31.1 °C for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the larva is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of 3 °C and 31 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for LBAM, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-lbam-parameters. Details on model parameterization are available at USPest.org (Barker et al. 2020). The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 7.2 °C and an upper developmental threshold of 31.1 °C to all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes that the larva is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies thresholds of 3 °C and 31 °C for cold and heat stress, respectively.

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
9B. Results

i. Phenology

Entire period: 1981–2025
Over 1981–2025, predicted first adult emergence and egg hatch generally occurred earlier across much of the southern and western United States, while later events were more apparent across portions of the northern interior (Figure 1, Figure 2). Significant changes occurred across broad portions of the eastern and central United States, with additional localized changes in the West.








Figure 1: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first adult emergence for LBAM across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.













Figure 2: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first egg hatch for LBAM across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.







Recent period: 2001–2025
During 2001–2025, earlier predicted phenology remained widespread across much of the West and central United States, while later events occurred in portions of the eastern and southern United States (Figure 3, Figure 4). Significant changes were more spatially limited than during the full period.








Figure 3: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first adult emergence for LBAM across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.













Figure 4: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first egg hatch for LBAM across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.








ii. Climatic suitability

Entire period: 1981–2025
Predicted cold stress decreased broadly across the northern United States over 1981–2025, while predicted heat stress increased across much of the western and southern United States and extended into portions of the eastern CONUS (Figure 5, Figure 6). These stress trends corresponded with relatively broad increases in predicted climatic suitability, particularly across portions of the central, southern, and eastern United States (Figure 7).








Figure 5: Changes (units/year) in predicted cold stress for LBAM across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 6: Changes (units/year) in predicted heat stress for LBAM across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 7: Changes in predicted climatic suitability for LBAM across the CONUS over the 44-year period (1981–2025). Suitability is defined as areas not excluded by climate stress. Positive changes (warmer colors) indicate an increased likelihood of establishment, whereas negative changes (cooler colors) indicate a decreased likelihood of establishment.







Recent period: 2001–2025
During 2001–2025, cold-stress changes remained mixed but decreases persisted in portions of the northern United States, while heat stress continued to increase across much of the CONUS (Figure 8, Figure 9). Significant suitability increases were more spatially limited than over the full period but remained evident in portions of the central and eastern United States (Figure 10).








Figure 8: Changes (units/year) in predicted cold stress for LBAM across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 9: Changes (units/year) in predicted heat stress for LBAM across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 10: Changes in predicted climatic suitability for LBAM across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Suitability is defined as areas not excluded by climate stress. Positive changes (warmer colors) indicate an increased likelihood of establishment, whereas negative changes (cooler colors) indicate a decreased likelihood of establishment.

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
9C. Discussion
The LBAM maps show broad changes in predicted phenology over the full period, with many regions experiencing earlier adult emergence and egg hatch. Because LBAM is a multivoltine pest whose development is strongly temperature dependent, earlier seasonal activity could increase the period during which populations can develop and reproduce in environmentally suitable areas. The recent-period maps show that these long-term patterns are not uniform through time, emphasizing the importance of considering both long-term trends and recent climate variability.
The combination of decreasing cold stress and increasing heat stress produced relatively broad changes in predicted climatic suitability over the full period. In northern regions, declining cold stress may reduce a major climatic constraint, whereas increasing heat stress in the warmest regions could offset potential suitability gains. The more limited recent-period suitability changes suggest that establishment potential has been comparatively stable in many regions during the shorter period.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

8A. Introduction
The Japanese pine sawyer beetle (JPSB), Monochamus alternatus Hope (Coleoptera: Cerambycidae), is a major vector of nematodes that cause pine wilt disease, particularly Bursaphelenchus xylophilus (Vicente et al. 2012, EPPO 2024). Native to East Asia, including mainland China, Taiwan, Laos, Korea, and Japan, JPSB has expanded its range to other parts of Asia, including Vietnam (Kobayashi et al. 1984, Ma et al. 2006, EPPO 2024). Adult beetles acquire and transmit nematodes while feeding on healthy pine trees, with infection disrupting xylem function and causing wilt and, in susceptible trees, death within weeks (Kobayashi et al. 1984, Vicente et al. 2012). Females primarily oviposit in weakened or diseased trees, where larvae develop beneath the bark and in the sapwood, nematodes subsequently associate with newly emerging adults, completing the transmission cycle (Kobayashi et al. 1984, Ma et al. 2006, An et al. 2019). Although B. xylophilus is native to North America and generally causes little damage in its native range, JPSB could also vector other nematode species not currently present in North America (CAPS 2013, An et al. 2019). JPSB primarily attacks conifers, particularly Pinus, Abies, Picea, Larix, and Cedrus, and pine wilt disease has caused extensive tree mortality and substantial economic losses where it has been introduced, particularly in Asia and Europe (Vicente et al. 2012, An et al. 2019).
Areas suitable for JPSB are predicted throughout much of the southern and midwestern United States, whereas cold temperatures may limit establishment in colder regions, including parts of the Intermountain West and Northeast (Song and Xu 2006, Barker and Coop 2020), Gao et al. 2023). Parts of the West Coast, including most of California, were also predicted to be suitable by some models (Song and Xu 2006, Barker and Coop 2020). Within environmentally suitable areas of the contiguous United States, JPSB is predicted to complete at least one generation annually, with up to four generations in the South (Barker and Coop 2020). In colder parts of its native range, JPSB may be univoltine or semivoltine, whereas 2–3 generations can occur annually in warmer regions such as subtropical and tropical China (Togashi 1989, Ma et al. 2006, CAPS 2013). JPSB undergoes winter diapause primarily during the final larval instar, with diapause induction influenced by larval density (Togashi 2021).
A model for Japanese pine sawyer beetle developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 12.2 °C and upper threshold of 35 °C for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the larva is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of −4 °C and 36 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for Japanese pine sawyer beetle, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-jpsb-parameters. Details on model parameterization are available at USPest.org (Barker and Coop 2020).

text:
8C. Discussion
The JPSB results indicate earlier phenology across many regions over the full period, with more limited and heterogeneous changes during 2001–2025. Because JPSB is associated with conifer hosts and its development is temperature dependent, regional shifts in emergence and egg hatch could alter the timing of detection and management activities. The stronger long-term pattern suggests that recent variability may be obscuring some of the longer-term directional signal.
The increase in predicted climatic suitability across portions of the northern United States over the full period is consistent with the concurrent decline in cold stress in those regions. This pattern suggests that warming may reduce cold-related limitations on establishment. During the recent period, increases in cold stress in parts of the northern interior corresponded with weaker suitability changes, illustrating how shorter-term regional climate patterns can alter the establishment signal.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
7A. Introduction
Native to Japan, the Japanese beetle (JPB), Popillia japonica Newman (Coleoptera: Scarabaeidae), is a highly polyphagous pest with a host range exceeding 400 plant species, including food crops, fruit trees, turfgrass, and ornamental plant (Fleming 1972, EPPO 2025, Tayeh et al. 2023). Since its initial detection in the United States in 1916 in New Jersey, JPB has spread widely across the eastern and central regions of the country, as well as parts of eastern Canada (Dickerson and Weiss 1918, Fleming 1972, EPPO 2025, Althoff and Rice 2022). Although isolated infestations have been successfully eradicated in several western states, including Nevada and California, the beetle persists in localized areas of the Pacific Northwest, including parts of Colorado, British Columbia, Washington, and Oregon (Althoff and Rice 2022, EPPO 2025, Stoven et al. 2021). Total associated costs of JPB in the United States are estimated at $460 million annually, with $234 million a year spent on control and turf replacement costs (Fleming 1972, USDA-APHIS 2015).
A model for JPB developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The full set of model parameters for JPB, including developmental temperature thresholds, degree-day requirements for individual life stages, and climate stress thresholds and limits, are available at USPest.org (Barker and Coop 2024).

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
7B. Results

i. Phenology

Entire period: 1981–2025
Predicted adult emergence and egg hatch for JPB shifted significantly earlier across large portions of CONUS over the entire period (1981–2025), including most East Coast states, parts of the southern and midwestern United States, and the Intermountain West (Figure 1, Figure 2). In these regions, predicted adult emergence and egg hatch decreased by approximately 0.01–0.5 days per year, with some of the largest declines occurring at higher elevations in the northeastern and western United States.








Figure 1: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first adult emergence for JPB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.













Figure 2: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first egg hatch for JPB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.







Recent period: 2001–2025
Trends in predictions of first adult emergence and egg hatch for JPB over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025) were partially consistent with those observed over the 1981–2025 period. In the eastern United States, significant trends were similar in magnitude but less spatially extensive (Figure 3, Figure 4), occurring mostly in East coast states and certain parts of the northern Midwest. Most trends in the western United States were not were not significant. In contrast to the longer-term trends, some isolated areas of the interior West, primarily in the southern Intermountain West, exhibited significant trends toward later phenological events.








Figure 3: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first adult emergence for JPB across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.













Figure 4: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first egg hatch for JPB across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.








ii. Climatic suitability

Entire period: 1981–2025
Significant trends in predicted cold stress for JPB over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025) were predominantly negative (Figure 5), indicating a general decrease in cold stress over time. In contrast, significant trends in heat stress were largely positive across portions of the South and West, indicating increasing heat stress (Figure 6). When annual accumulated stress units exceed limits specified in DDRP models, climatic suitability may change. Consistent with these trends, suitability for JPB increased in Minnesota, but decreased in portions of the Southwest (Figure 7). However, these changes were statistically significant only in parts the Southwest and California, suggesting that changes in predicted heat stress may reduce the likelihood of JPB establishment in these areas.








Figure 5: Changes (units/year) in predicted cold stress for JPB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 6: Changes (units/year) in predicted heat stress for JPB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 7: Changes in predicted climatic suitability for JPB across the CONUS over the 44-year period (1981–2025). Suitability is defined as areas not excluded by climate stress. Positive changes (warmer colors) indicate an increased likelihood of establishment, whereas negative changes (cooler colors) indicate a decreased likelihood of establishment.







Recent period: 2001–2025
Statistically significant trends in predicted heat and cold stress for JPB during the recent period (2001–2025) were more spatially limited than those observed over the entire period (1981–2025) (Figure 8, Figure 9). Areas with significant increases in heat stress were generally consistent between the two periods, whereas several areas that exhibited significant decreases in cold stress over the entire period, including the Great Lakes region, no longer showed significant trends. Conversely, parts of the Great Plains and Rocky Mountains exhibited significant increases in cold stress during the recent period. Trends in predicted climatic suitability were broadly consistent with those observed over the entire period but were less spatially extensive, with significant decreases in suitability confined to isolated areas of the Southwest and California, where heat stress increased (Figure 10).








Figure 8: Changes (units/year) in predicted cold stress for JPB across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 9: Changes (units/year) in predicted heat stress for JPB across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 10: Changes in predicted climatic suitability for JPB across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Suitability is defined as areas not excluded by climate stress. Positive changes (warmer colors) indicate an increased likelihood of establishment, whereas negative changes (cooler colors) indicate a decreased likelihood of establishment.

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
7C. Discussion
Because JPB is widely established across much of the East and Midwest, trends toward earlier predicted adult emergence and egg hatch could have practical implications for monitoring and management. Pest managers may need to adjust the timing of seasonal activities to maintain their effectiveness. For example, traps targeting adult beetles may need to be deployed earlier to improve early detection of new infestations, while insecticide treatments targeting larvae may need to be applied earlier because first- and second-instar larvae are more susceptible to insecticides than older larvae. Similarly, releases of larval parasitoids, such as Tiphia vernalis (Rohwer), may need to be timed to coincide with earlier larval development.
A trend toward earlier phenological events could increase the likelihood of univoltinism in cooler regions. Although JPB is generally univoltine in the United States, semivoltinism has been reported in colder areas, such as New England, where larvae overwinter a second winter as second or third instars in the soil, typically beneath managed turfgrass (Fleming 1972, Vittum 1986). Consistent with field observations, a CLIMEX model predicted univoltinism across most of the beetle’s current North American range, but semivoltinism in the Northeast and along the United States–Canada border (Kistner-Thomas 2019).
Although cold stress declined for JPB in northern and high-elevation regions of the CONUS, these changes did not translate into significant shifts in predicted establishment risk. However, previous research linked JPB occurrence at its expanding range edge in the Midwest and Great Plains to minimum temperatures and long-term weather trends (Kucherov et al. 2025), suggesting that changes in cold stress could influence its distribution over time. Declining cold stress may also reduce the effectiveness of Ovavesicula popilliae, a microsporidian biocontrol agent that increases JPB larval mortality under cold overwintering conditions (Smitley et al. 2026). In contrast, Kucherov et al. (2025) found negative associations between JPB occurrence and maximum temperature, consistent with our finding of significant declines in predicted climatic suitability across the Southwest and California, where heat stress increased over both the entire (1981–2025) and recent (2001–2025) periods. These declines also align with evidence that JPB survival is low under hot, dry conditions ( Fleming 1972, Vittum 1986, Allsopp 1996).
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the entire 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: Assessing the potential impacts of weather changes on pest activities and establishment
text:
i. Overview of DDRP
The mechanics of DDRP are detailed in Barker et al. (2020). Briefly, DDRP uses a process-based modeling approach in which degree-days and climate stress are calculated daily and accumulate over time to model phenology and climatic suitability, respectively (Figure 1 A). Required inputs include gridded daily minimum and maximum temperature data for a time frame of interest and a species parameter file. Models include four separate life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) plus a separately parameterized overwintering stage. Phenology models often incorporate variation in phenology using a user-defined number of time-distributed cohorts that reflect the distribution of times in which the overwintering stage completes development.
DDRP uses annual accumulated climate stress units to identify two levels of temperature-based exclusion: moderate and severe. Similar to degree-days, which accumulate temperatures above a developmental threshold, climate stress units accumulate when temperatures exceed specified stress thresholds for heat or fall below thresholds for cold. The greater the accumulated stress units, the greater the potential for temperature-related exclusion. Locations not excluded by either level of stress are considered part of the potential distribution and have the highest potential for establishment based on temperature alone. Moderate stress may limit long-term establishment, although short-term establishment may still occur during favorable years. Severe stress is expected to prevent even short-term establishment, defined as survival for one complete year. Because the model considers temperature alone, it does not account for host availability or other environmental factors that may influence pest distributions.
Over the daily time-step, DDRP produces outputs that include maps of the potential distribution, number of generations, life stages present, and dates of phenological events. Additionally, it integrates maps produced by the phenology and climatic suitability model to provide insight into phenology (i.e., life stage present or the date of specific event) only in areas at risk of establishment.








Figure 1: Workflow for producing maps for the DDRP Pest Trends web application. (A) Daily minimum and maximum temperatures (1981–2025) and species-specific model parameters served as inputs to the Degree-Days, Risk, and Phenological Event Mapping (DDRP) system. (B) DDRP models estimate pest phenology, including adult emergence and egg hatch, and climatic suitability based on cold and heat stress, which together inform potential distribution. (C) Time series analyses compare trends over the full 1981–2025 period and the more recent 2001–2025 period. (D) Individual-species outputs characterize trend direction, statistical significance, and magnitude of change. (E) Summary statistics across 18 invasive pest species identify geographic areas with consistent trends in phenology and climatic suitability.

title: Assessing the potential impacts of weather changes on pest activities and establishment
section: ii. Trend analyses for individual species
text:
ii. Trend analyses for individual species
Five types of predictions produced by DDRP were retained for trend analyses for this study: (1) dates (day of year) of first adult emergence, (2) dates of first egg hatch, (3) cold stress accumulation, (4) heat stress accumulation, and (5) the potential distribution, as measured by areas not excluded by cold and heat stresses (Figure 1 B). Modeling in DDRP used daily minimum and maximum temperature data for 1981 to 2025 at 4-kmsuperscript2 resolution from the PRISM (Parameter-elevation Relationships on Independent Slopes Model) (Daly et al. 1994, 2008) database (http://www.prism.oregonstate.edu).
We evaluated the direction and magnitude of changes in predictions over two periods: 1981–2025 (the full 44-year period) and 2001–2025 (the recent 25-year period; Figure 1 C). Analyzing both periods allowed us to characterize long-term trends and determine whether more recent changes in predicted phenology and climatic suitability differed from patterns observed over the longer period. Trends were assessed using the Mann–Kendall test and Theil–Sen regression, two rank-based, non-parametric methods widely used for analyzing environmental and remotely sensed time series (Goossens and Berger 1986). These methods do not require normally distributed data and are therefore suitable for environmental variables that may depart from a normal distribution. The Mann–Kendall test identifies whether an increasing or decreasing trend exists and assesses its statistical significance (Mann 1945, Kendall 1975, Gilbert 1987). Kendall’s tau quantifies the direction and strength of the trend, ranging from −1 (strong negative trend) to +1 (strong positive trend). Trends were considered statistically significant at P < 0.10, a threshold often used in spatial analyses of environmental and remotely sensed time series to identify potentially meaningful trends while accounting for variability in climatic data (Wang et al. 2020).
Theil–Sen regression estimates the rate of change over time as the median slope across all pairs of observations. Slopes are expressed in the relevant units per year: days per year for phenological events and cumulative climate stress units per year for cold and heat stress. For phenology, negative slopes indicate that developmental events are occurring earlier, whereas positive slopes indicate later timing. These shifts may affect seasonal activity, survival, reproduction, and establishment potential, depending on the species and its life history. Changes in annual climate stress units indicate whether temperature stress is increasing or decreasing over time. As accumulated stress units rise above predefined limits in DDRP, locations may shift from suitable to moderately or severely stress-excluded. Conversely, declining stress may allow locations to become climatically suitable as accumulated units fall below these limits. Decreasing cold stress may improve winter survival and allow range expansion into previously unsuitable areas, whereas increasing heat stress may reduce summer survival and limit establishment.
The Mann-Kendall and Theil-Sen analyses were implemented in the R package modifiedmk v. 1.6 (Patakamuri 2021) and used predictions that were corrected for serial correlation (autocorrelation) using the approach of von Storch (1995) and Kulkarni and von Storch (1995). This correction for autocorrelation, also known as “prewhitening,” is often applied to avoid violating the Mann-Kendall test’s assumption of no autocorrelation in the time series, which may increase the likelihood of type 1 error (rejecting the null hypothesis when it might be true) (Kulkarni and von Storch 1995, Yue et al. 2002, Zhang and Zwiers 2004). The accumulation of degree-days and climate stresses in our models exhibits a seasonal cycle driven by temperature, which would increase autocorrelation in the time series (Coen et al. 2020).
A cumulative link model (CLM) was used to assess temporal changes in predicted climate suitability for establishment, represented by three ordinal categories of climate-stress exclusion: no exclusion, moderate exclusion, and severe exclusion (Barker et al. 2020). The model estimates temporal trends in the probability of a location falling into each suitability category. Positive trends indicate a shift toward no exclusion, consistent with decreasing temperature-related stress and potentially more favorable conditions for establishment. Conversely, negative trends indicate a shift toward moderate or severe exclusion, consistent with increasing temperature-related stress and potentially less favorable conditions for establishment. The CLM was fitted in R using the ordinal package (v. 2023.12-4) (Christensen 2025), with a logit link function and the proportional odds assumption. Model coefficients (β) were used to assess the direction and magnitude of temporal trends, and corresponding P-values were used to evaluate statistical significance. Positive coefficients indicate a shift toward lower climate stress and greater potential for establishment, whereas negative coefficients indicate a shift toward greater climate stress and lower potential for establishment. Coefficients are expressed on the log-odds scale and are not restricted to a fixed range.

title: Assessing the potential impacts of weather changes on pest activities and establishment
text:
iii. Comparative analyses
Outputs from trend analyses for the 18 species (Figure 1 D) were combined to identify areas where pests consistently exhibited earlier first adult emergence and first egg hatch, decreasing cold stress, and increasing heat stress (Figure 1 E). Spatial descriptive statistics were calculated across species, including the mean and variance in the magnitude of change and the frequency of statistically significant increasing versus decreasing trends. Analyses were conducted separately for 1981–2025 and 2001–2025 to characterize spatial patterns in long-term trends and determine whether more recent trends differed from those observed over the longer period.
