title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
4A. Introduction
The emerald ash borer (EAB), Agrilus planipennis Fairmaire (Coleoptera: Buprestidae), is a flat-headed, wood-boring beetle native to eastern Asia that relies almost exclusively on ash trees (Fraxinus species) to complete its life cycle (Poland et al. 2015, USDA-APHIS 2025). It was first detected in North America in 2002 in Michigan and Ontario, although it likely arrived in Michigan during the early to mid-1990s (Siegert et al. 2014). EAB is now present in 37 U.S. states and six Canadian provinces (EPPO 2025, USDA-APHIS 2025). Adult beetles lay eggs in bark crevices, and upon hatching, larvae burrow into the tree to feed on the inner phloem, outer xylem, and cambium. They overwinter as larvae or pre-pupae within characteristic serpentine galleries beneath the bark (Tluczek et al. 2011, Poland et al. 2015). This feeding disrupts the tree’s ability to transport water and nutrients, typically leading to tree death within several years (Knight et al. 2013). EAB’s cryptic nature, in which all life stages except for the adult beetle are inside of trees, makes early detection of this pest extremely difficult (Haack et al. 2002, USDA-APHIS 2025).
Previous modeling studies indicated broad climatic suitability for EAB across North America that overlapped with the ranges of native Fraxinus species (DeSantis et al. 2013, Sobek-Swant et al. 2012, Liang & Fei 2014, , Barker et al. 2023). All North American ash species are vulnerable to EAB, though blue ash (F. quadrangulata Michaux) appears to be less preferred (Poland et al. 2015). In its native range, the beetle primarily infests stressed or weakened trees, whereas in North America it readily attacks both healthy and stressed individuals, with stressed trees often supporting higher beetle densities (Poland and McCullough 2006, Tluczek et al. 2011). Other members of the olive family, such as white fringetree (Chionanthus virginicus L.) and olive (Olea europaea L.), may also serve as hosts, though survival rates on these species appear to be lower (Rutledge and Arango-Velez 2017, Peterson and Cipollini 2020). The economic impact of EAB in the United States has reached billions of dollars, and the widespread loss of ash trees has led to reduced biodiversity and the degradation of important ecosystem services (Kovacs et al. 2010, Aukema et al. 2011, Schrader et al. 2021).
A model for EAB developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The full set of model parameters for EAB, including developmental temperature thresholds, degree-day requirements for individual life stages, and climate stress thresholds and limits, are available at USPest.org (Barker et al. 2023).

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
4B. Results

i. Phenology

Entire period: 1981–2025
Predicted adult emergence and egg hatch for JPB shifted significantly earlier across large portions of CONUS over the entire period (1981–2025), including most East Coast states and parts of the South and Intermountain West (Figure 1, Figure 2). In these regions, predicted adult emergence and egg hatch decreased by approximately 0.01–0.9 days per year, with some of the largest declines occurring at higher elevations in the Intermountain West. Significant changes were more spatially extensive for predicted egg hatch, encompassing much of the central United States.








Figure 1: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first adult emergence for EAB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.













Figure 2: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first egg hatch for EAB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.







Recent period: 2001–2025
Trends in predictions of first adult emergence and egg hatch for EAB over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025) were partially consistent with those observed over the 1981–2025 period. In the East, significant trends were similar in magnitude but less spatially extensive (Figure 3, Figure 4), whereas most trends in the West were not significant. In contrast to the longer-term trends, parts of the northern Great Plains showed significant shifts toward earlier adult emergence, whereas isolated areas of the interior West, primarily in the southern Intermountain West, exhibited significant trends toward later phenological events.








Figure 3: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first adult emergence for EAB across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.













Figure 4: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first egg hatch for EAB across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.








ii. Climatic suitability

Entire period: 1981–2025
Over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025), predicted cold stress for EAB decreased significantly across portions of the northern United States, particularly the Upper Midwest, although localized increases occurred in parts of Montana (Figure 5). During the same period, predicted heat stress increased significantly across parts of the South and West (Figure 6). When annual accumulated stress units exceed limits specified in DDRP models, climatic suitability may change. Significant shifts in climatic suitability for EAB were relatively limited, indicating that accumulated stress generally remained within the limits defining suitability. Increases in suitability were concentrated in portions of the Southwest (Figure 7).








Figure 5: Changes (units/year) in predicted cold stress for EAB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 6: Changes (units/year) in predicted heat stress for EAB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 7: Changes in predicted climatic suitability for EAB across the CONUS over the 44-year period (1981–2025). Suitability is defined as areas not excluded by cold and heat stress. Positive changes (warmer colors) indicate an increased likelihood of establishment, whereas negative changes (cooler colors) indicate a decreased likelihood of establishment.







Recent period: 2001–2025
Trends in climate stress for EAB over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025) differed in several respects. Predicted cold stress increased across portions of the Upper Midwest, with few areas showing significant decreases (Figure 8), contrasting with the widespread decreases observed over the longer period. Heat stress continued to increase across the Southwest and Lower Midwest but decreased in parts of the interior West, southern California, and Arizona (Figure 9). As during the longer period, changes in climatic suitability remained spatially localized, suggesting that recent shifts in cold and heat stress translated into relatively limited changes in predicted establishment suitability (Figure 10).








Figure 8: Changes (units/year) in predicted cold stress for EAB across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 9: Changes (units/year) in predicted heat stress for EAB across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 10: Changes in predicted climatic suitability for EAB across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Suitability is defined as areas not excluded by cold and heat stress. Positive changes (warmer colors) indicate an increased likelihood of establishment, whereas negative changes (cooler colors) indicate a decreased likelihood of establishment.

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
4C. Discussion
Predicted EAB phenology generally shifted toward earlier seasonal events, with the strongest and most spatially extensive trends occurring over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Predicted adult emergence and egg hatch occurred progressively earlier across portions of the East during both study periods, at rates of approximately 0.01–0.9 days per year. Because EAB is widely established across much of this region, these shifts have practical implications for monitoring and management. Pest managers may need to adjust the timing of seasonal activities to maintain their effectiveness. For example, traps targeting adult beetles may need to be deployed earlier in spring to improve early detection of new infestations, while release schedules for biological control agents, including the larval parasitoids Spathius agrili and S. galinae, may need to be adjusted to account for changes in host availability.
In contrast, significant trends toward later adult emergence and egg hatch occurred in parts of the Intermountain West during 2001–2025. These localized patterns may reflect regional differences in temperature trends and seasonal warming, which have not been spatially or seasonally uniform across the United States (NCEI 2021). However, further analysis of temperature trends during the study period is needed to determine whether these differences explain the predicted delays.
Trends in EAB’s phenology should be interpreted in light of some current limitations of the phenology model. First, the model predicts adult emergence solely from degree-day accumulation and does not account for the chilling requirements of overwintering J-larvae, which must receive sufficient winter chilling to terminate obligatory diapause before metamorphosis can begin (Duan et al. 2021, Duan et al. 2026). Because warmer chilling temperatures may delay adult emergence (Duan et al. 2026), the model may overestimate advances in emergence in warmer regions of the United States, including the South. Second, the model assumes a univoltine life cycle, whereas EAB can exhibit a semivoltine life cycle in cooler regions, overwintering as early instars and requiring a second summer of feeding before reaching the J-larval stage (Jones et al. 2019, Bohannon et al. 2022). This extended development may alter the timing and distribution of adult emergence relative to model predictions. Incorporating chilling requirements and regional variation in voltinism could therefore improve the accuracy of predicted phenological trends and their application to monitoring and biological control.
The limited changes in predicted climatic suitability across both time periods indicate that trends in cold and heat stress have not produced broad changes in predicted EAB establishment potential across the CONUS. Although decreasing cold stress across portions of the Upper Midwest could potentially enhance overwintering survival in EAB, it did not substantially increase predicted establishment potential in these regions. Conversely, increasing heat stress in the Southwest may constrain establishment in already warm regions, particularly where it overlaps with the ranges of native Fraxinus species. The lack of substantial increases in predicted suitability in the Upper Midwest is consistent with previous findings that only sufficiently extreme cold, such as that experienced in parts of northern Canada, is likely to limit EAB establishment through overwintering mortality (Venette et al. 2014, Barker et al. 2023). From a management perspective, these findings support continuing EAB surveillance across the CONUS rather than substantially narrowing surveillance efforts based on the observed trends in climatic suitability.
Our findings were broadly consistent with Barker et al. (2023), who reported geographically restricted trends toward earlier predicted first adult emergence of EAB over 2002–2021, including in parts of the Southeast, New England, and Upper Midwest. Our analysis also identified significant trends toward later adult emergence in parts of the interior West over 2001–2025. Both studies identified isolated areas of decreasing climatic suitability in the southwestern United States, consistent with increasing heat stress. Differences between the studies may partly reflect methodological differences, particularly our use of pre-whitening to account for temporal autocorrelation in the Mann–Kendall analysis. Pre-whitening reduces temporal autocorrelation to better satisfy the test’s assumption of independence among observations and can affect the magnitude and spatial extent of statistically significant trends (Kulkarni and von Storch 1995).
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the entire 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: Comparative analysis
text:
Results

i. Phenology

Entire period: 1981–2025

First adult emergence
Main differences among species - SLF, SLI, and CGN show relatively extensive areas of trends toward earlier predicted adult emergence, particularly across portions of the West and the southern and eastern United States. SLF has a broad distribution of earlier trends, whereas SLI shows a more pronounced contrast between later trends in the north and earlier trends farther south. - LBAM and SLYM show a particularly clear north–south contrast, with trends toward later emergence across portions of the northern United States and earlier emergence farther south and east. - FCM and ASRB also exhibit this contrast, with later trends concentrated in parts of the northern interior and earlier trends across portions of the South and East. The distribution and extent of significant trends differ between the two species. - STB shows a more spatially heterogeneous pattern, with substantial variation across the West and contrasting trends between northern and southern regions. Significant changes occur in scattered areas rather than forming one continuous region. - JPSB shows a notable contrast between later trends in portions of the northern interior West and earlier trends in the eastern United States, where significant changes are more apparent. - SUNP and PTLM show northern areas of later trends and southern or western areas of earlier trends, although significant changes are more spatially restricted than the overall patterns suggest. - OWBW and OAB generally show weaker, more localized patterns, with much of the mapped area exhibiting relatively small changes and significant trends occurring in scattered locations. - JPB, ECW, and EAB also show predominantly weak or spatially fragmented patterns of change, although localized areas of significant earlier emergence occur in parts of the West and South. - ALB differs in presentation from the other species maps, so its spatial pattern should be compared cautiously until the corresponding map format and trend metric are confirmed.
The clearest distinction is between species with relatively extensive, geographically coherent trends toward earlier emergence (particularly SLF, SLI, and CGN) and those with weaker or more spatially fragmented patterns (including OWBW, OAB, ECW, and EAB). LBAM, SLYM, FCM, and ASRB show especially noticeable contrasts between northern areas with later trends and southern or eastern areas with earlier trends. Importantly, the areas showing trends in the full maps are more extensive than the areas showing statistically significant changes, so these patterns should not be interpreted as uniformly significant across each region.


First egg hatch
Main differences among species - STB, TABS, ALB, and OAB show relatively extensive trends toward earlier egg hatch across portions of the West and southern United States. STB and OAB exhibit particularly broad areas of earlier trends, whereas TABS shows a stronger contrast between earlier trends in the West and later trends in portions of the North. - SLI and SLF show a pronounced north–south contrast, with later egg hatch across much of the northern United States and earlier egg hatch across portions of the West and South. This pattern is particularly extensive in SLI and SLF. - LBAM, SUNP, ASRB, CGN, ECW, and OWBW show generally weaker trends across much of the eastern United States, with localized areas of earlier or later egg hatch, particularly in the West. The spatial extent of significant changes varies among these species. - FCM and SLYM show relatively extensive areas of later egg hatch in portions of the northern United States, contrasting with earlier trends across parts of the West and South. - EAB and JPB show more extensive trends toward earlier egg hatch across portions of the West and South, with localized later trends in the northern interior. Significant changes extend across portions of the Pacific coast and southern United States. - JPSB shows a more mixed pattern, with earlier egg hatch across parts of the West and later egg hatch in portions of the northern interior, although the overall magnitude of change is generally modest. Manuscript-ready synthesis
Trends in predicted egg hatch over 1981–2025 varied among species in both direction and geographic extent. SLI and SLF exhibited pronounced north–south contrasts, with later egg hatch across much of the northern United States and earlier egg hatch across portions of the West and South. In contrast, STB, TABS, ALB, and OAB showed more extensive trends toward earlier egg hatch across portions of the West and southern United States. FCM and SLYM showed relatively pronounced areas of later egg hatch in the northern United States, whereas LBAM, SUNP, ASRB, CGN, ECW, and OWBW generally exhibited weaker or more localized trends. EAB and JPB showed earlier egg hatch across portions of the West and South, with localized areas of later trends in the northern interior. Across species, the extent of statistically significant changes varied substantially, indicating that broad spatial patterns of change were not uniformly significant.



Recent period: 2001–2025

First adult emergence
The 2001–2025 adult-emergence maps show an important shift in the geographic pattern compared with 1981–2025. Whereas the longer-term results generally showed significant advances concentrated in the eastern United States, the recent-period maps more often show a contrast between earlier predicted emergence across the West and northern interior and later emergence across portions of the East and South. However, the extent of statistically significant changes varies among species.
Main differences from 1981–2025 - SLF and SLI: The recent-period maps show a stronger contrast between earlier emergence across portions of the West and later emergence in the eastern United States. This differs from the more extensive eastern advances evident over the longer period. - LBAM and SLYM: Both show a pronounced west–east contrast in the recent period, with earlier emergence across portions of the West and later emergence farther east. This pattern is more spatially differentiated than the predominantly earlier trends described for the full period. - FCM and ASRB: The recent maps show earlier emergence across portions of the western and central United States, contrasting with later emergence in parts of the East and South. The recent pattern therefore differs from the longer-term concentration of significant advances in the eastern United States. - STB and TABS: Both show extensive spatial variation in recent trends, including earlier emergence across portions of the West and northern interior. Their recent patterns appear more heterogeneous than a simple, widespread advance in emergence. - CGN, EAB, ECW, and JPB: The recent maps show earlier emergence across portions of the West and central United States, but significant changes are comparatively localized. This suggests that the geographic extent of recent changes differs from the broader long-term patterns. - OWBW, OAB, SUNP, and PTLM: Recent trends are generally spatially variable, with localized areas of earlier emergence and portions of the East showing later trends. Significant changes are relatively restricted in these maps. - JPSB: The recent map shows a distinct contrast between earlier emergence in parts of the West and later emergence in portions of the East, with relatively localized significant changes. - ALB: The recent map shows substantial spatial variation, including areas of both earlier and later emergence. Its pattern should be interpreted separately from the other species until the corresponding long-term map is directly compared.
Overall interpretation The most notable difference is that the recent 25-year period shows a more pronounced west–east contrast in predicted adult-emergence trends for several species, whereas the 44-year period was characterized by significant advances across large portions of the eastern United States. This suggests that the spatial distribution of phenological change during 2001–2025 does not simply reproduce the longer-term pattern. Instead, recent trends vary more strongly among regions and species, with earlier emergence concentrated in portions of the West and later emergence in parts of the East and South.


First egg hatch
The most notable difference is a shift in the geographic distribution of egg-hatch trends. In the 2001–2025 maps, later predicted egg hatch is more apparent across portions of the western and central United States, whereas earlier egg hatch is more apparent across portions of the East and Northeast. This contrasts with the longer-term maps for several species, which showed earlier egg hatch across portions of the West and South. Main differences among species - SLI and SLYM: Both show a pronounced contrast between later egg hatch across portions of the West and central United States and earlier egg hatch in the East. This differs from the longer-term patterns, which showed later egg hatch concentrated more strongly in the North and earlier egg hatch across portions of the West and South. - TABS and STB: The recent maps show later egg hatch across substantial portions of the West and central United States, contrasting with earlier trends in portions of the East. This differs from the broader western and southern advances described for the longer period. - FCM: Later egg hatch is prominent across parts of the central United States in the recent period, contrasting with the longer-term pattern of later hatch in the North and earlier hatch across parts of the West and South. - LBAM and SUNP: The recent maps show a clearer contrast between later egg hatch across portions of the West and earlier hatch in parts of the East. This suggests that the recent spatial pattern differs from the generally weaker or more localized long-term trends. - ASRB, CGN, ECW, and OWBW: The recent maps show later egg hatch across parts of the West and central United States, with earlier hatch in portions of the East. These patterns are more regionally differentiated than the weaker or more localized long-term trends. - OAB and JPSB: Both show a mixture of earlier and later trends, with later hatch across portions of the West and earlier hatch in parts of the East. The recent patterns appear more spatially differentiated than the longer-term results. - PTLM: The recent map shows later egg hatch in portions of the West and central United States, contrasting with earlier hatch in parts of the East. Significant changes remain relatively localized. - JPB and EAB: Both show mixed trends, with later egg hatch across portions of the West and earlier hatch in parts of the East and Northeast. The recent patterns differ from the broader western and southern advances described for the longer period. - ALB: The recent map shows a distinct pattern of earlier egg hatch across much of the eastern United States, particularly the Northeast, contrasting with later trends in portions of the West. This is a notable regional contrast, although the ALB map uses a different presentation from the other species.
Overall interpretation Across species, the 2001–2025 egg-hatch maps suggest a more pronounced west–east contrast than the 1981–2025 maps. Later egg hatch is more apparent across portions of the West and central United States, whereas earlier egg hatch is more apparent in parts of the East and Northeast. This contrasts with the longer-term tendency toward earlier egg hatch across portions of the West and South in several species. The degree of this shift varies among species, and statistically significant trends occupy smaller, more localized areas than the overall mapped trends.

title: 3. Honeydew Moth (Cryptoblabes gnidiella)
text:
3A. Introduction
Native to the Mediterranean region, the honeydew moth, Cryptoblabes gnidiella (CGN) (Lepidoptera: Pyralidae), can act as both a primary and secondary pest of numerous economically important crops, including avocado, citrus, corn, cotton, grape, loquat, pomegranate, rice, and wheat throughout Asia, Oceania, the Middle East, and Europe (Silva and Mexia 1999, Molet 2013). It is commonly associated with coccoids and pseudococcids, which produce honeydew that serves as a food source for its larvae, although it can also directly damage the fruit of certain host plants (Avidov and Gothilf 1960, Yehuda et al. 1991, Silva and Mexia 1999, Molet 2013). The species has spread widely across southern Europe, parts of Africa, and several regions worldwide, including Brazil, Fiji, India, Malaysia, New Zealand, Uruguay, and Hawaii in the United States (EPPO 2025, Molet 2013). Although it has not become established in the contiguous United States (CONUS), it is frequently intercepted at ports of entry, often originating from countries where its establishment has not been documented (Molet 2013, Velez-Gavilan 2023).
A model for CGN developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the CONUS at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The full set of model parameters for CGN, including developmental temperature thresholds, degree-day requirements for individual life stages, and climate stress thresholds and limits, are available at USPest.org (Barker and Coop 2019).

title: 3. Honeydew Moth (Cryptoblabes gnidiella)
text:
3B. Results

i. Phenology

Entire period: 1981–2025
Trends in predicted first adult emergence and egg hatch for CGN over the 44-year period (1981–2025) were predominantly negative, indicating that both phenological events shifted earlier over time. Earlier phenology was spatially extensive, occurring across most of the CONUS (Figure 1, Figure 2). Statistically significant trends were more spatially restricted, occurring primarily in portions of the southern and eastern United States and in scattered areas of the West. Within these regions, predicted adult emergence and egg hatch shifted earlier by approximately 0.01–0.8 days per year, with some of the largest shifts occurring at higher elevations in the West. Trends toward later phenology occurred in a some isolated areas of the West but most were not statistically significant.








Figure 1: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first adult emergence for CGN across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.













Figure 2: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first egg hatch for CGN across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.







Recent period: 2001–2025
Trends in predictions of first adult emergence and egg hatch for CGN over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025) were partially consistent with those observed over the 1981–2025 period. Significant trends towards earlier phenology were similar in magnitude but less spatially extensive, occurring predominantly in parts of the upper Midwest, Northeast, and Southeast (Figure 3, Figure 4). In contrast, areas exhibiting trends toward later phenological events were somewhat larger and more spatially extensive across the West.








Figure 3: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first adult emergence for CGN across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.













Figure 4: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first egg hatch for CGN across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.








ii. Climatic suitability

Entire period: 1981–2025
Over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025), predicted cold stress for CGN decreased across broad portions of the CONUS, with the strongest changes occurring in the Northeast, upper Midwest, and Intermountain West (Figure 5). However, trends across the Great Plains and South were generally smaller and mostly nonsignificant. Predicted heat stress increased across much of the West, southern Great Plains, and parts of the Southeast, although significant trends were concentrated primarily in the West (Figure 6). However, changes in stress units for CGN did not correspond to significant shifts in climatic suitability across the CONUS (Figure 7), indicating that accumulated stress generally remained within the limits defining CGN’s climatic suitability.








Figure 5: Changes (units/year) in predicted cold stress for CGN across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 6: Changes (units/year) in predicted heat stress for CGN across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 7: Changes in predicted climatic suitability for CGN across the CONUS over the 44-year period (1981–2025). Suitability is defined as areas not excluded by cold and heat stress. Positive changes (warmer colors) indicate an increased likelihood of establishment, whereas negative changes (cooler colors) indicate a decreased likelihood of establishment.







Recent period: 2001–2025
Many areas that exhibited significant decreases in cold stress for CGN over 1981–2025 no longer showed significant trends during the recent period. These areas were concentrated in scattered patches across the East and South and at higher elevations in the West (Figure 8). Significant increases in predicted cold stress occurred in a few small, isolated areas of the West. Significant increases in heat stress were concentrated in the South, particularly Texas, whereas parts of California showed significant decreases (Figure 9). As in the 1981–2025 analysis, changes in cold and heat stress did not produce significant changes in climatic suitability (Figure 10).








Figure 8: Changes (units/year) in predicted cold stress for CGN across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 9: Changes (units/year) in predicted heat stress for CGN across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 10: Changes in predicted climatic suitability for CGN across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Suitability is defined as areas not excluded by cold and heat stress. Positive changes (warmer colors) indicate an increased likelihood of establishment, whereas negative changes (cooler colors) indicate a decreased likelihood of establishment.

title: 3. Honeydew Moth (Cryptoblabes gnidiella)
text:
3C. Discussion
Although CGN is not established in the CONUS, understanding predicted changes in phenology can inform surveillance planning. In areas exhibiting significant trends toward earlier phenology, predicted dates shifted earlier by approximately 0.01–0.8 days per year, suggesting that surveillance materials may need to be deployed earlier in the season. Surveillance efforts may be particularly important where these trends overlap with major host-fruit production areas, including those supporting intensive cultivation of grapes, citrus, pomegranates, and avocados. Such areas include parts of the West and South, particularly California and Texas, as well as portions of the Gulf Coast.
Earlier adult emergence and egg hatch could potentially allow CGN to complete more generations per year, increasing pest pressure and associated crop damage. CGN lacks a true winter diapause and can complete multiple generations under warm conditions (Avidov and Gothilf 1960, Molet 2013, Lucchi et al. 2019). The number of generations completed annually therefore depends partly on whether local environmental conditions permit continued development throughout the growing season. CGN can complete as many as nine generations annually in the warmest parts of its range, such as northeastern Brazil (Ringenberg et al. 2005, Ioriatti et al. 2012, Molet 2013, Öztürk 2018, Lucchi et al. 2019, Corbetta et al. 2025). DDRP predictions indicate that CGN may complete at least one generation annually and up to eight generations in the South within climatically suitable areas (Barker and Coop 2019). These findings underscore the importance of interpreting regional trends in predicted phenology alongside climatic suitability and the potential for multiple generations, which together determine the timing and duration of seasonal CGN activity.
The climate-stress trend maps showed broad changes in both cold and heat stress, but these changes translated into statistically significant shifts in predicted climatic suitability for ECW in only a few isolated areas of California and the Southwest. The contrast between widespread climate-stress trends and limited suitability changes suggests that the modeled climatic limits remain sufficiently broad that changes in individual stress variables do not necessarily alter establishment potential. Previous modeling studies for CGN identified suitable environments for the pest throughout the South and Midwest, as well as along the West Coast, whereas cold temperatures would likely exclude the pest from colder regions, including the Intermountain West and latitudes north of ca. 41° N in the East (Barker and Coop 2019, Zumbado-Ulate et al. 2023). The results of this study suggest that these areas have remained suitable for CGN establishment over the study periods. However, a recent modeling study predicted increasing climatic suitability for CGN in the Mediterranean region, with suitable conditions shifting northward along the region’s northern margins. These findings highlight the need for further investigation into potential shifts in CGN establishment risk across the CONUS (Rossi et al. 2026).
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the entire 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: 2. Asiatic rice borer (Chilo suppressalis)
text:
2A. Introduction
The Asiatic rice borer (ASRB), Chilo suppressalis Walker (Lepidoptera: Crambidae), is a stem borer and major pest of rice and other grasses, including water oat, sorghum, millet, and corn, throughout Asia, Oceania, the Middle East, and Europe (CAPS 2025, Meng et al. 2008). ASRB larvae cause major damage to rice crops by severing panicles or the vascular system of tillers, leading to white earheads and dead hearts (Kiritani and Iwao 1967, Muralidharan and Pasalu 2006, Chen et al. 2014, EPPO 2019). Larvae can cause substantial economic losses, with reports of 20% yield loss under some conditions (Rahman et al. 2004). The pest is present in Hawaii and is frequently intercepted at United States ports of entry (Solis 2006). With the United States rice industry valued at over USD 6 billion in 2025 (Childs 2025), yield reductions resulting from ASRB could cause significant economic damage to rice-producing regions.
A model for ASRB developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The full set of model parameters for ASRB, including developmental temperature thresholds, degree-day requirements for individual life stages, and climate stress thresholds and limits, are available at USPest.org (Coop and Barker 2020).

Statistically significant trends were more spatially restricted, occurring primarily in the East, the South, and higher elevations of the West. Within these regions, predicted adult emergence and egg hatch shifted earlier by approximately 0.01–0.5 days per year, with some of the largest shifts occurring at higher elevations in the West. title: 2. Asiatic rice borer (Chilo suppressalis)
text:
2C. Discussion
Although ASRB is not established in the CONUS, understanding predicted changes in phenology can inform surveillance planning. In areas with earlier phenological events, predicted dates shifted earlier by approximately 0.01–0.5 days per year, suggesting that surveillance materials may need to be deployed earlier in the season. The southern United States warrants particular attention because it includes major rice-producing states, such as Louisiana, Texas, and Arkansas, where surveillance could help detect potential introductions into areas with suitable host crops.
Although warmer growing-season temperatures can advance ASRB emergence and increase voltinism, temperature effects on development and overwintering are context dependent. ASRB is univoltine in cooler parts of its native range, such as northern Japan, where shortening day lengths serve as the primary environmental cue for larvae to enter winter diapause. In contrast, populations in warmer regions, including Taiwan, can complete 5–6 generations annually and typically lack diapause (Kiritani and Iwao 1967, Ramoneda and Roig 1993, Tsumuki et al. 1994). Genetic differentiation among ASRB populations in China is also associated with geographic variation in voltinism (Meng et al. 2008). Warmer growing-season temperatures have been linked to earlier emergence and spring flight, increased voltinism (Lee 2014), and greater pupal weight and fecundity (Fu et al. 2016, Huang et al. 2018). However, experimental studies found that warmer winter temperatures (10 °C versus 1 and 5 °C) reduced pupation rates, pupal weight, and post-diapause reproductive potential (Xiao et al. 2017). Collectively, these findings suggest that the effects of temperature on ASRB development and population dynamics depend on seasonal conditions and geographic context, underscoring the importance of considering both phenological shifts and climatic suitability when prioritizing surveillance.
The climate-stress maps showed regional changes in both cold and heat stress, but these changes produced little statistically significant change in predicted climatic suitability. This distinction is important because changes in individual stress variables do not necessarily translate into changes in establishment likelihood when the modeled conditions remain within the suitable range. Decreasing cold stress in portions of the northern United States and could reduce a temperature-related limitation on establishment, whereas increasing heat stress in parts of the Southwest and California could impose greater climatic constraints. However, because the climatic-suitability maps showed very few significant changes, these stress trends did not translate into widespread changes in predicted establishment likelihood.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the entire 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: 1. Asian longhorned beetle (Anoplophora glabripennis)
text:
1A. Introduction
The Asian longhorned beetle (ALB), Anoplophora glabripennis Motschulsky (Coleoptera: Cerambycidae), is a wood-eating pest native to the Korean peninsula and eastern China. In the United States, the beetle was first discovered on Long Island, NY, in 1996, where it likely arrived via wood packaging from China (Haack and Hoebeke 1996). The pest spread to several sites in the eastern United States and Canada but has since been eradicated in Illinois, New Jersey, New York City, Boston, and Canada (Coyle et al. 2021, EPPO 2019). However, infestations currently persist in central Long Island, NY; Worcester County, MA; Clermont County, OH; and Charleston County, SC (Coyle et al. 2021, USDA-APHIS 2025). ALB is a major threat to the maple hardwood lumber and sugar maple syrup industries, as well as tourism associated with fall colors in maple trees (Smith and Wu 2008). The cost of a complete infestation of all urban areas in the United States has been estimated at $669 billion (Nowak et al. 2001).
An estimated 30-35% of trees in the eastern United States are species commonly attacked by ALB (Nowak et al. 2001, Smith and Wu 2008). The pest can complete its lifecycle on Acer, Aesculus, Albizia julibrissin, Betula, Cercidiphyllum, Elaeagnus angustifolia, Fraxinus, Platanus, Populus, Salix, Sorbus aucuparia and Ulmus species (van der Gaag and Loomans 2014). However, preferred genera in North America are Acer and Ulmus, compared to Populus and Salix in China (Hu et al. 2009, van der Gaag and Loomans 2014). Following oviposition under the bark of host trees, larvae feed in the cambial region before burrowing into the inner xylem and heartwood (Haack and Hoebeke 1996, Haack 2006). ALB may overwinter as an egg, larva, or pupa, though typically as an egg or larva, before emerging from round exit holes as adults (Haack and Hoebeke 1996, Haack 2006, Herard et al. 2009, Faccoli et al. 2015, Trotter and Keena 2016). Diapause termination requires a chilling period, and larvae may be freeze tolerant (Roden et al. 2008, Torson et al. 2021).
A model for ALB developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The full set of model parameters for ALB, including developmental temperature thresholds, degree-day requirements for individual life stages, and climate stress thresholds and limits, are available at USPest.org (Coop 2018).

title: 1. Asian longhorned beetle (Anoplophora glabripennis)
text:
1B. Results

i. Phenology

Entire period: 1981–2025
Significant trends in predicted first adult emergence and egg hatch for ALB over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025) were predominantly negative, indicating that these phenological events shifted earlier over time (Figure 1, Figure 2). Significant advances were concentrated across large portions of the eastern United States, with additional localized areas along the Pacific coast, in the South, and at higher elevations of the interior West. In these regions, predicted adult emergence and egg hatch decreased by approximately 0.01–0.8 days per year, with some of the largest declines occurring at higher elevations in the West.








Figure 1: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first adult emergence for ALB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.













Figure 2: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first egg hatch for ALB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.







Recent period: 2001–2025
Trends in predictions of first adult emergence and egg hatch for ALB during the recent 24-year period (2001–2025) were generally consistent with those observed over the 44-year period, although changes were smaller in magnitude and less spatially extensive (Figure 3, Figure 4). For example, significantly earlier adult emergence and egg hatch were predicted primarily in parts of the eastern United States, with only isolated areas of significant change elsewhere in the CONUS.








Figure 3: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first adult emergence for ALB across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps depict the trend in predicted dates, significance of the trend (P-value), and change in predicted dates (days/year). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.













Figure 4: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first egg hatch for ALB across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.








ii. Climatic suitability

Entire period: 1981–2025
Significant trends in predicted cold stress for ALB over the full 44-year period (1981–2025) were predominantly negative (Figure 5), indicating a general decrease in cold stress over time. In contrast, significant trends in heat stress were largely positive across portions of the Southwest, indicating increasing heat stress (Figure 6). When annual accumulated stress units exceed limits specified in DDRP models, climatic suitability may change. Consistent with these trends, suitability for ALB increased in parts of the Midwest, including Minnesota and North Dakota, but decreased in southern California and adjacent desert regions (Figure 7). However, only some of these changes were statistically significant, suggesting that shifts in climatic suitability were spatially limited.








Figure 5: Changes (units/year) in predicted cold stress for ALB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 6: Changes (units/year) in predicted heat stress for ALB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 7: Changes in predicted climatic suitability for ALB across the CONUS over the 44-year period (1981–2025). Suitability is defined as areas not excluded by cold and heat stress. Positive changes (warmer colors) indicate an increased likelihood of establishment, whereas negative changes (cooler colors) indicate a decreased likelihood of establishment.







Recent period: 2001–2025
Statistically significant trends in predicted heat and cold stress for ALB over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025) were more spatially limited than those observed over the entire 1981–2025 period (Figure 8, Figure 9). Areas with significant increases in heat stress were generally consistent with those identified for the entire period, whereas several areas with significant decreases in cold stress over 1981–2025 showed no significant trend during 2001–2025. Additionally, parts of the Midwest and Rocky Mountains exhibited significant increases in cold stress, although the magnitude of these changes was small. Consistent with these patterns, fewer areas with significant changes in climatic suitability were identified, indicating that the predicted likelihood of establishment was relatively stable during the recent recent period (Figure 10).








Figure 8: Changes (units/year) in predicted cold stress for ALB across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 9: Changes (units/year) in predicted heat stress for ALB across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 10: Changes in predicted climatic suitability for ALB across CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Suitability is defined as areas not excluded by cold and heat stress. Positive changes (warmer colors) indicate an increased likelihood of establishment, whereas negative changes (cooler colors) indicate a decreased likelihood of establishment.

title: 1. Asian longhorned beetle (Anoplophora glabripennis)
text:
1C. Discussion
Predictions of phenology and climatic suitability for ALB show clear, directional changes, with the strongest and most spatially extensive signals emerging over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Predicted adult emergence and egg hatch occurred progressively earlier across large portions of CONUS, averaging 0.01–0.5 days earlier per year, which suggests that surveyors and other management staff in these areas may want to ensure that materials are prepared earlier in the season. Faster development under warmer conditions could also enable ALB to achieve more rapid population growth, increase its damage potential, and shorten or eliminate the pupal hold period, potentially increasing the likelihood of multiple generations per year (Schmitt et al. 2025a,b).
Declines in predicted cold stress across northern and high-elevation regions—including parts of the Northeast and Midwest—may indicate increasing potential for overwinter survival in ALB. These regions may be especially vulnerable because of the high abundance of preferred host species for ALB, particularly maple (Smith and Wu 2008; Berland and Elliot 2014). Thus, surveyors and managers may want to increase the prioritization of areas such as northern New England and Michigan. Although significant increases in heat stress—and corresponding reductions in establishment risk—are predicted for the hottest parts of the Southwest, risk in this region is likely already constrained by the relatively low density of hardwood forests.
The stronger and more significant trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the entire 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. For example, increases in predicted cold stress in parts of the north-central United States may reflect this region’s departure from the broader warming pattern during the more recent period, with some areas experiencing cooler conditions relative to the preceding years (NCEI 2021).

title: About
text:
Overview
We use the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological (DDRP) event mapping system to assess the potential impacts of weather from 1980 to the current year on the timing of pest activity such as emergence (phenology) and potential for establishment of 18 invasive pest species in the contiguous United States.






TipOpen to see more info on the 18 species





Of the 18 species with models, 12 are presently on Plant Protection and Quarantine’s National Priority Pest List. Six were formerly included on the list, and two are Federal Program Pests. Most of the species do not occur in the contiguous United States (N = 13); however, five are established and may spread to additional regions. Real-time forecasts for these pests are available at USPEST.org.

The system is part of a suite of decision-support tools at USPEST.org that are developed and maintained by the Oregon Integrated Pest Management Center (OIPMC) at Oregon State University. These tools provide thousands of end users nationwide with information to support timely and effective management activities for agricultural pests and diseases. This project will use the DDRP event mapping system to predict where pests may exhibit earlier activities, increases in the number of generations, and increases in habitat suitability. This information helps Plant Protection and Quarantine allocate survey resources more strategically, thereby reducing the likelihood of pest establishment and spread.
The DDRP event mapping system is distinct from existing pest decision-support systems in its combination of

integrated phenology and habitat suitability mapping to fully address both when and where a pest life stage may occur over a year,
incorporation of biologically meaningful parameters that increase model realism in contrast with simple degree-day models, and
inclusion of survival-limiting cold and heat stresses to predict habitat suitability over a year, whereas most other systems use simpler models based on weather averages (Barker et al. 2020; Grevstad et al. 2022; Barker et al. 2023).

Additionally, its ability to accept daily weather data for any time frame allows evaluation of historical conditions and impacts of weather changes on pest phenology and establishment.

title: DDRP Pest Trends: User Guide
text:
The Degree-Day, Establishment Risk, and Phenological (DDRP) Pest Trends web app was developed by modelers at the Oregon Integrated Pest Management Center at Oregon State University. It provides interactive maps and location-specific plots for exploring trends in predicted pest phenology and climate stress across the contiguous United States (CONUS).
The app currently provides model outputs for 18 invasive pest species (Table 1). It can help users explore where predicted pest activity and climate stress have changed over time. The results can inform further investigation, monitoring, and management planning, but should be interpreted in the context of the underlying models. For more information about individual species and how results may be applied to management, visit the Pest Reports page and consult the report for the species of interest. The full report provides additional details about the study objectives, modeling methods, and analyses underlying the results.

title: DDRP Pest Trends: User Guide
text:
Requirements
The app requires an internet connection and a device with a web browser. It is designed to adjust to different screen sizes and can be used on a desktop computer, laptop, tablet, or smartphone. Common browsers include Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, and Microsoft Edge. Open the web app at https://riskmaps.oregonstate.edu/DDRP_pest_trends/.

title: DDRP Pest Trends: User Guide
text:
Getting started
When you open the DDRP Pest Trends web app, the landing page introduces the application, its purpose, and the pest species with DDRP models (Fig. 1). Review this information to understand the scope of the app, the types of pest trends you can explore.





Figure 1. DDRP Pest Trends landing page. Letters identify the three main subpages: (A) About this site, (B) DDRP Map, and (C) Pest Reports. The landing page provides an overview of the application, tutorial, source code, contact information, and additional resources.




From the landing page, navigate to the DDRP Map page to explore the model outputs. The map displays using the default selections, with the available controls located on the left side of the interface (Fig. 2). Use these controls to select a pest species, geographic region, variable type, trend metric, and time range. The map, summary statistics, and location-specific plots update according to your selections.





Figure 2. Overview of the DDRP Pest Trends interface. Letters identify the main controls and outputs: (A) insect pest selection, (B) geographic region, (C) variable type, (D) phenology metric, (E) time range, (F) map panel, (G) color legend, (H) significance filter, (I) map download, (J) location-specific summary statistics, and (K) location-specific trend plot. The significance filter displays only areas with statistically significant trends (P < 0.1).

title: DDRP Pest Trends: User Guide
text:
Menu panel: Select map options

Pest species
Use the Select insect pest dropdown menu to choose an individual species or All species (comparison) (Fig. 2A). When an individual species is selected, you can examine trends in its phenology, climate stress, or suitability. For species-specific context, including map interpretation and management implications, see the corresponding report on the Pest Reports page.
When All species (comparison) is selected, you can identify areas where trends are consistent across the 18 species, including earlier predicted pest activities and increasing climatic suitability. The full report on the Pest Reports page describes spatial patterns observed across species and provides further interpretation of these results.


Region
Use the Select region dropdown menu to choose the geographic area displayed on the map (Fig. 2B). Selecting a state zooms the map to that area. The default selection is the CONUS.


Variable type
Choose the type of information to display using the Select variable type dropdown menu (Fig. 2C):

Phenology describes the predicted timing of pest life-cycle events.
Climate stress describes predicted temperature-related stress that may affect pest survival.
Suitability describes predicted climatic suitability, defined as areas not excluded by temperature-related stress.



Phenology metric
This dropdown menu appears when Phenology is selected (Fig. 2D).

First Adult Emergence: The predicted timing of first adult emergence.
First Egg Hatch: The predicted timing of first egg hatch.



Climate variable
This dropdown menu appears when Climate stress is selected (Fig. 2D).

Cold Stress: Displays trends in predicted cold stress.
Heat Stress: Displays trends in predicted heat stress.



Suitability
Climatic suitability represents potential pest establishment based on temperature-related stress.


Time range
Use the Select time range dropdown menu to choose the period used for trend analysis (Fig. 2E).

1981–2025: The the entire 44-year period.
2001–2025: The recent 24-year period.

title: DDRP Pest Trends: User Guide
text:
Map panel: Explore trend maps

Viewing and interpreting trend maps

Individual species
Each map for an individual species shows the spatial distribution of the selected trend metric across the chosen region (Fig. 2F). In the legend, Sen’s slope measures the amount and direction of change per year (Fig. 2G). It is expressed in days per year for phenology or units per year for cold and heat stress. Values near zero indicate little estimated change, positive values indicate an increase over time, and negative values indicate a decrease. For phenology, negative values indicate earlier predicted events, whereas positive values indicate later predicted events (Fig. 3). For climate stress, negative values indicate decreasing stress, while positive values indicate increasing stress (Fig. 4).





Figure 3. Changes (days/year) in predicted first adult emergence for spotted lanternfly across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025).









Figure 4. Changes (units/year) in predicted cold stress for spotted lanternfly across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025).




Decreasing cold stress may increase climatic suitability for a pest and its potential for establishment, whereas increasing heat stress may decrease suitability (Fig. 5). Changes in suitability were assessed using a cumulative link model based on DDRP’s three temperature-stress exclusion categories: no exclusion (0), moderate exclusion (−1), and severe exclusion (−2). Positive coefficients indicate a shift toward higher suitability (0), whereas negative coefficients indicate a shift toward lower suitability (−2). To view only areas with statistically significant changes, select the Show significant areas only checkbox.





Figure 5. Changes in predicted climatic suitability for spotted lanternfly across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025).




Comparing maps produced for the 1981–2025 and 2001–2025 periods helps distinguish long-term trends from more recent changes (Fig. 6). Consider the direction and magnitude of trends, the geographic extent of statistically significant changes, and the consistency of patterns between periods. Differences may reflect changes in climate patterns, interannual variability, or statistical power and do not, on their own, identify the causes of observed trends.





Figure 6. Trends in predicted first adult emergence of spotted lanternfly across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981-2025) for (A) all trends and (B) statistically significant trends only (P < 0.1). Negative values indicate earlier predicted emergence, whereas positive values indicate later predicted emergence.






All species (comparison)
Outputs from trend analyses for the 18 species were combined to identify areas where pests consistently exhibited earlier first adult emergence and first egg hatch, decreasing cold stress, and increasing heat stress. Spatial descriptive statistics were calculated across species, including the mean and variance in the magnitude of change and the frequency of statistically significant increasing versus decreasing trends.
In Figure 7, the map shows the geographic distribution of agreement among 18 invasive pest species in significant trends toward earlier predicted dates of first adult emergence across the CONUS during the 44-year period (1981–2025). Higher values indicate locations where more species exhibited statistically significant advances in predicted adult emergence, highlighting regions where earlier seasonal pest activity is a consistent cross-species pattern.





Figure 7. Cross-species comparison of significant trends in predicted dates of first adult emergence across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981-2025). Colors indicate the number of species exhibiting statistically significant trends (P < 0.1) toward earlier first adult emergence at each location.







Downloading maps
Use the Download map button to export a map for your area of interest (Fig. 2I). Before exporting, select the desired pest species, variable, region, time range, and other display options. Exporting a map may take several seconds and, in some cases, nearly a half-minute to complete. Please allow time for the export process to finish.

title: DDRP Pest Trends: User Guide
text:
Location-based information

Individual species
The Summary statistics panel for individual species provides information about trends at the selected location for the selected pest species and variable (Figs. 2J and 8). Content in this panel appears after a location is selected by clicking on the map. The summary statistics include:

Change (days/year or units/year): Sen’s slope estimates the rate and direction of change over time. Positive values indicate an increase, while negative values indicate a decrease.
Trend direction and strength: Kendall’s tau (τ) indicates the direction and strength of a monotonic trend. Positive values indicate an upward trend, negative values indicate a downward trend, and values near 0 indicate a weak or absent monotonic trend.
P-value: The Mann–Kendall test assesses whether a monotonic trend is statistically significant. A P-value < 0.1 indicates a statistically significant trend.






Figure 8. Location-based summary statistics and time-series plot of trends in predicted first adult emergence for spotted lanternfly at a selected location in North Carolina over the entire 44-year period (1981-2025). Summary statistics include the estimated rate of change in emergence date (days/year), the direction and strength of trend (Kendall’s tau), and the associated P-value. The time-series plot shows annual predicted emergence dates and the fitted linear trend; a negative slope indicates a shift toward earlier predicted emergence.




Selecting a location also produces a plot showing predicted values over time at that location (Fig. 2K). Use the Download plot button to export the plot. The time-series plot includes:

Predicted values: The model-predicted value for each year at the selected location.
Red line: The estimated linear trend (slope) over time.
P-value: An indication of the statistical significance of the trend.

Missing points in the plot should not automatically be interpreted as missing weather observations. For the selected event, they may reflect the model’s assessment that conditions were unsuitable for the event to occur.

All species (comparison)
For the cross-species comparison, selecting a location displays summary statistics describing the number of species with significant trends and the magnitude of change in phenology or climate stress at that location (Fig. 9):

Significant trends (no. species): Number of species with significant trends at the selected location.
Median slope: The median rate of change across the 18 species, expressed in days per year for phenology or units per year for climate stress.
Slope range: The minimum and maximum rates of change across species, indicating the variability in trend magnitude and direction.

The comparison plot summarizes these trends, with the black point indicating the median slope, the blue bar representing the median ± standard error, and gray error bars showing the minimum-to-maximum slope range (Fig. 9). Negative slopes indicate earlier predicted phenological events or decreasing climate stress, whereas positive slopes indicate later phenological events or increasing climate stress. The range of slopes helps users assess the variability in trends among species at the selected location.





Figure 9. Location-based summary statistics and comparison plot for first adult emergence across 18 invasive pest species over the entire 44-year period (1981-2025). The map shows the number of species exhibiting statistically significant trends toward earlier predicted adult emergence at the selected location in Maryland.

title: DDRP Pest Trends: User Guide
text:
Using results for pest management
Consult the full report, including species-specific reports, on the Pest Reports page for guidance on applying results to pest management. Before making management decisions:

Consider the direction and magnitude of the trend, not only statistical significance.
Interpret predictions in the context of local conditions and other relevant information.
Use model outputs as decision-support information, not as direct observations of pest abundance or confirmation of establishment.

title: DDRP Pest Trends: User Guide
text:
Important considerations

Model predictions are not direct observations. The results reflect predictions from the underlying DDRP models and their associated assumptions, rather than direct observations of pest activity or establishment risk. The observed trends do not, on their own, establish the causes of the predicted changes.
Statistical significance is not the same as practical importance. A small trend can be statistically significant, and a large estimated trend may not be statistically significant.
Missing points have a specific interpretation. In the time-series plots, they indicate conditions unsuitable for the selected event to occur.
Results depend on the selected settings. Confirm the pest, variable type, metric, region, and time range before interpreting results.
Temperature-driven trends do not account for all factors influencing pest dynamics. The models are driven by temperature, so the mapped trends reflect changes in temperature and their effects on predicted pest phenology and climate stress. However, the maps do not capture the effects of other factors that may influence pest activity, survival, or establishment.
