title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
1A. Introduction
The Asian longhorned beetle (ALB), Anoplophora glabripennis Motschulsky (Coleoptera: Cerambycidae), is a wood-eating pest native to the Korean peninsula and eastern China. In the United States, the beetle was first discovered on Long Island, NY, in 1996, where it likely arrived via wood packaging from China (Haack and Hoebeke 1996). The pest spread to several sites in the eastern United States and Canada but has since been eradicated in Illinois, New Jersey, New York City, Boston, and Canada (Coyle et al. 2021, EPPO 2019). However, infestations currently persist in central Long Island, NY; Worcester County, MA; Clermont County, OH; and Charleston County, SC (Coyle et al. 2021, USDA-APHIS 2025). ALB is a major threat to the maple hardwood lumber and sugar maple syrup industries, as well as tourism associated with fall colors in maple trees (Smith and Wu 2008). The cost of a complete infestation of all urban areas in the United States has been estimated at $669 billion (Nowak et al. 2001).
An estimated 30-35% of trees in the eastern United States are species commonly attacked by ALB (Nowak et al. 2001, Smith and Wu 2008). The pest can complete its lifecycle on Acer, Aesculus, Albizia julibrissin, Betula, Cercidiphyllum, Elaeagnus angustifolia, Fraxinus, Platanus, Populus, Salix, Sorbus aucuparia and Ulmus species (van der Gaag and Loomans 2014). However, preferred genera in North America are Acer and Ulmus, compared to Populus and Salix in China (Hu et al. 2009, van der Gaag and Loomans 2014). Following oviposition under the bark of host trees, larvae feed in the cambial region before burrowing into the inner xylem and heartwood (Haack and Hoebeke 1996, Haack 2006). ALB may overwinter as an egg, larva, or pupa, though typically as an egg or larva, before emerging from round exit holes as adults (Haack and Hoebeke 1996, Haack 2006, Herard et al. 2009, Faccoli et al. 2015, Trotter and Keena 2016). Diapause termination requires a chilling period, and larvae may be freeze tolerant (Roden et al. 2008, Torson et al. 2021).
A model for ALB developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The full set of model parameters for ALB, including developmental temperature thresholds, degree-day requirements for individual life stages, and climate stress thresholds and limits, are available at USPest.org (Coop 2018).

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
1B. Results

i. Phenology

Entire period: 1981–2025
Significant trends in predicted first adult emergence and egg hatch for ALB over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025) were predominantly negative, indicating that these phenological events shifted earlier over time (Figure 1, Figure 2). Significant advances were concentrated across large portions of the eastern United States, with additional localized areas along the Pacific coast, in the South, and at higher elevations of the interior West. In these regions, predicted adult emergence and egg hatch decreased by approximately 0.01–0.8 days per year, with some of the largest declines occurring at higher elevations in the West.








Figure 1: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first adult emergence for ALB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.













Figure 2: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first egg hatch for ALB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.







Recent period: 2001–2025
Trends in predictions of first adult emergence and egg hatch for ALB during the recent 24-year period (2001–2025) were generally consistent with those observed over the 44-year period, although changes were smaller in magnitude and less spatially extensive (Figure 3, Figure 4). For example, significantly earlier adult emergence and egg hatch were predicted primarily in parts of the eastern United States, with only isolated areas of significant change elsewhere in the CONUS.








Figure 3: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first adult emergence for ALB across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps depict the trend in predicted dates, significance of the trend (P-value), and change in predicted dates (days/year). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.













Figure 4: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first egg hatch for ALB across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.








ii. Climatic suitability

Entire period: 1981–2025
Significant trends in predicted cold stress for ALB over the full 44-year period (1981–2025) were predominantly negative (Figure 5), indicating a general decrease in cold stress over time. In contrast, significant trends in heat stress were largely positive across portions of the Southwest, indicating increasing heat stress (Figure 6). When annual accumulated stress units exceed limits specified in DDRP models, climatic suitability may change. Consistent with these trends, suitability for ALB increased in parts of the Midwest, including Minnesota and North Dakota, but decreased in southern California and adjacent desert regions (Figure 7). However, only some of these changes were statistically significant, suggesting that shifts in climatic suitability were spatially limited.








Figure 5: Changes (units/year) in predicted cold stress for ALB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 6: Changes (units/year) in predicted heat stress for ALB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 7: Changes in predicted climatic suitability for ALB across the CONUS over the 44-year period (1981–2025). Suitability is defined as areas not excluded by cold and heat stress. Positive changes (warmer colors) indicate an increased likelihood of establishment, whereas negative changes (cooler colors) indicate a decreased likelihood of establishment.







Recent period: 2001–2025
Statistically significant trends in predicted heat and cold stress for ALB over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025) were more spatially limited than those observed over the entire 1981–2025 period (Figure 8, Figure 9). Areas with significant increases in heat stress were generally consistent with those identified for the entire period, whereas several areas with significant decreases in cold stress over 1981–2025 showed no significant trend during 2001–2025. Additionally, parts of the Midwest and Rocky Mountains exhibited significant increases in cold stress, although the magnitude of these changes was small. Consistent with these patterns, fewer areas with significant changes in climatic suitability were identified, indicating that the predicted likelihood of establishment was relatively stable during the recent recent period (Figure 10).








Figure 8: Changes (units/year) in predicted cold stress for ALB across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 9: Changes (units/year) in predicted heat stress for ALB across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 10: Changes in predicted climatic suitability for ALB across CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Suitability is defined as areas not excluded by cold and heat stress. Positive changes (warmer colors) indicate an increased likelihood of establishment, whereas negative changes (cooler colors) indicate a decreased likelihood of establishment.

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
1C. Discussion
Predictions of phenology and climatic suitability for ALB show clear, directional changes, with the strongest and most spatially extensive signals emerging over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Predicted adult emergence and egg hatch occurred progressively earlier across large portions of CONUS, averaging 0.01–0.5 days earlier per year, which suggests that surveyors and other management staff in these areas may want to ensure that materials are prepared earlier in the season. Faster development under warmer conditions could also enable ALB to achieve more rapid population growth, increase its damage potential, and shorten or eliminate the pupal hold period, potentially increasing the likelihood of multiple generations per year (Schmitt et al. 2025a,b).
Declines in predicted cold stress across northern and high-elevation regions—including parts of the Northeast and Midwest—may indicate increasing potential for overwinter survival in ALB. These regions may be especially vulnerable because of the high abundance of preferred host species for ALB, particularly maple (Smith and Wu 2008; Berland and Elliot 2014). Thus, surveyors and managers may want to increase the prioritization of areas such as northern New England and Michigan. Although significant increases in heat stress—and corresponding reductions in establishment risk—are predicted for the hottest parts of the Southwest, risk in this region is likely already constrained by the relatively low density of hardwood forests.
The stronger and more significant trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the entire 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. For example, increases in predicted cold stress in parts of the north-central United States may reflect this region’s departure from the broader warming pattern during the more recent period, with some areas experiencing cooler conditions relative to the preceding years (NCEI 2021).

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
2A. Introduction
The Asiatic rice borer (ASRB), Chilo suppressalis Walker (Lepidoptera: Crambidae), is a stem borer and major pest of rice and other grasses, including water oat, sorghum, millet, and corn, throughout Asia, Oceania, the Middle East, and Europe (CAPS 2025, Meng et al. 2008). ASRB larvae cause major damage to rice crops by severing panicles or the vascular system of tillers, leading to white earheads and dead hearts (Kiritani and Iwao 1967, Muralidharan and Pasalu 2006, Chen et al. 2014, EPPO 2019). Larvae can cause substantial economic losses, with reports of 20% yield loss under some conditions (Rahman et al. 2004). The pest is present in Hawaii and is frequently intercepted at United States ports of entry (Solis 2006). With the United States rice industry valued at over USD 6 billion in 2025 (Childs 2025), yield reductions resulting from ASRB could cause significant economic damage to rice-producing regions.
A model for ASRB developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The full set of model parameters for ASRB, including developmental temperature thresholds, degree-day requirements for individual life stages, and climate stress thresholds and limits, are available at USPest.org (Coop and Barker 2020).

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
2B. Results

i. Phenology

Entire period: 1981–2025
Trends in predicted first adult emergence and egg hatch for ASRB over the 44-year period (1981–2025) were predominantly negative, indicating that both phenological events shifted earlier over time. Earlier phenology was spatially extensive, occurring across much of the CONUS, although trends toward later phenology occurred in portions of the northern interior and western United States (Figure 1, Figure 2). Statistically significant trends were more spatially restricted, occurring primarily in the East, the South, and higher elevations of the West. Within these regions, predicted adult emergence and egg hatch shifted earlier by approximately 0.01–0.5 days per year, with some of the largest shifts occurring at higher elevations in the West. Only a few small, isolated areas exhibited significant trends towards later phenology.








Figure 1: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first adult emergence for ASRB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.













Figure 2: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first egg hatch for ASRB across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.







Recent period: 2001–2025

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
2C. Discussion
Although ASRB is not established in the CONUS, understanding predicted changes in phenology can inform surveillance planning. In areas with earlier phenological events, predicted dates shifted earlier by approximately 0.01–0.5 days per year, suggesting that surveillance materials may need to be deployed earlier in the season. The southern United States warrants particular attention because it includes major rice-producing states, such as Louisiana, Texas, and Arkansas, where surveillance could help detect potential introductions into areas with suitable host crops.
Although warmer growing-season temperatures can advance ASRB emergence and increase voltinism, temperature effects on development and overwintering are context dependent. ASRB is univoltine in cooler parts of its native range, such as northern Japan, where shortening day lengths serve as the primary environmental cue for larvae to enter winter diapause. In contrast, populations in warmer regions, including Taiwan, can complete 5–6 generations annually and typically lack diapause (Kiritani and Iwao 1967, Ramoneda and Roig 1993, Tsumuki et al. 1994). Genetic differentiation among ASRB populations in China is also associated with geographic variation in voltinism (Meng et al. 2008). Warmer growing-season temperatures have been linked to earlier emergence and spring flight, increased voltinism (Lee 2014), and greater pupal weight and fecundity (Fu et al. 2016, Huang et al. 2018). However, experimental studies found that warmer winter temperatures (10 °C versus 1 and 5 °C) reduced pupation rates, pupal weight, and post-diapause reproductive potential (Xiao et al. 2017). Collectively, these findings suggest that the effects of temperature on ASRB development and population dynamics depend on seasonal conditions and geographic context, underscoring the importance of considering both phenological shifts and climatic suitability when prioritizing surveillance.
The climate-stress maps showed regional changes in both cold and heat stress, but these changes produced little statistically significant change in predicted climatic suitability. This distinction is important because changes in individual stress variables do not necessarily translate into changes in establishment likelihood when the modeled conditions remain within the suitable range. Decreasing cold stress in portions of the northern United States and could reduce a temperature-related limitation on establishment, whereas increasing heat stress in parts of the Southwest and California could impose greater climatic constraints. However, because the climatic-suitability maps showed very few significant changes, these stress trends did not translate into widespread changes in predicted establishment likelihood.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the entire 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
3A. Introduction
Native to the Mediterranean region, the honeydew moth, Cryptoblabes gnidiella (CGN) (Lepidoptera: Pyralidae), can act as both a primary and secondary pest of numerous economically important crops, including avocado, citrus, corn, cotton, grape, loquat, pomegranate, rice, and wheat throughout Asia, Oceania, the Middle East, and Europe (Silva and Mexia 1999, Molet 2013). It is commonly associated with coccoids and pseudococcids, which produce honeydew that serves as a food source for its larvae, although it can also directly damage the fruit of certain host plants (Avidov and Gothilf 1960, Yehuda et al. 1991, Silva and Mexia 1999, Molet 2013). The species has spread widely across southern Europe, parts of Africa, and several regions worldwide, including Brazil, Fiji, India, Malaysia, New Zealand, Uruguay, and Hawaii in the United States (EPPO 2025, Molet 2013). Although it has not become established in the contiguous United States (CONUS), it is frequently intercepted at ports of entry, often originating from countries where its establishment has not been documented (Molet 2013, Velez-Gavilan 2023).
A model for CGN developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the CONUS at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The full set of model parameters for CGN, including developmental temperature thresholds, degree-day requirements for individual life stages, and climate stress thresholds and limits, are available at USPest.org (Barker and Coop 2019).

3B. Results

i. Phenology

Entire period: 1981–2025
Trends in predicted first adult emergence and egg hatch for CGN over the 44-year period (1981–2025) were predominantly negative, indicating that both phenological events shifted earlier over time. Earlier phenology was spatially extensive, occurring across most of the CONUS (Figure 1, Figure 2). Statistically significant trends were more spatially restricted, occurring primarily in portions of the southern and eastern United States and in scattered areas of the West. Within these regions, predicted adult emergence and egg hatch shifted earlier by approximately 0.01–0.8 days per year, with some of the largest shifts occurring at higher elevations in the West. Trends toward later phenology occurred in a some isolated areas of the West but most were not statistically significant.

Significant trends towards earlier phenology were similar in magnitude but less spatially extensive, occurring predominantly in parts of the upper Midwest, Northeast, and Southeast (Figure 3, Figure 4). In contrast, areas exhibiting trends toward later phenological events were somewhat larger and more spatially extensive across the West.

Entire period: 1981–2025
Over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025), predicted cold stress for CGN decreased across broad portions of the CONUS, with the strongest changes occurring in the Northeast, upper Midwest, and Intermountain West (Figure 5). However, trends across the Great Plains and South were generally smaller and mostly nonsignificant. Predicted heat stress increased across much of the West, southern Great Plains, and parts of the Southeast, although significant trends were concentrated primarily in the West (Figure 6). However, changes in stress units for CGN did not correspond to significant shifts in climatic suitability across the CONUS (Figure 7), indicating that accumulated stress generally remained within the limits defining CGN’s climatic suitability.

title: DDRP Pest Trends
text:
3C. Discussion
Although CGN is not established in the CONUS, understanding predicted changes in phenology can inform surveillance planning. In areas exhibiting significant trends toward earlier phenology, predicted dates shifted earlier by approximately 0.01–0.8 days per year, suggesting that surveillance materials may need to be deployed earlier in the season. Surveillance efforts may be particularly important where these trends overlap with major host-fruit production areas, including those supporting intensive cultivation of grapes, citrus, pomegranates, and avocados. Such areas include parts of the West and South, particularly California and Texas, as well as portions of the Gulf Coast.
Earlier adult emergence and egg hatch could potentially allow CGN to complete more generations per year, increasing pest pressure and associated crop damage. CGN lacks a true winter diapause and can complete multiple generations under warm conditions (Avidov and Gothilf 1960, Molet 2013, Lucchi et al. 2019). The number of generations completed annually therefore depends partly on whether local environmental conditions permit continued development throughout the growing season. CGN can complete as many as nine generations annually in the warmest parts of its range, such as northeastern Brazil (Ringenberg et al. 2005, Ioriatti et al. 2012, Molet 2013, Öztürk 2018, Lucchi et al. 2019, Corbetta et al. 2025). DDRP predictions indicate that CGN may complete at least one generation annually and up to eight generations in the South within climatically suitable areas (Barker and Coop 2019). These findings underscore the importance of interpreting regional trends in predicted phenology alongside climatic suitability and the potential for multiple generations, which together determine the timing and duration of seasonal CGN activity.
The climate-stress trend maps showed broad changes in both cold and heat stress, but these changes translated into statistically significant shifts in predicted climatic suitability for ECW in only a few isolated areas of California and the Southwest. The contrast between widespread climate-stress trends and limited suitability changes suggests that the modeled climatic limits remain sufficiently broad that changes in individual stress variables do not necessarily alter establishment potential. Previous modeling studies for CGN identified suitable environments for the pest throughout the South and Midwest, as well as along the West Coast, whereas cold temperatures would likely exclude the pest from colder regions, including the Intermountain West and latitudes north of ca. 41° N in the East (Barker and Coop 2019, Zumbado-Ulate et al. 2023). The results of this study suggest that these areas have remained suitable for CGN establishment over the study periods. However, a recent modeling study predicted increasing climatic suitability for CGN in the Mediterranean region, with suitable conditions shifting northward along the region’s northern margins. These findings highlight the need for further investigation into potential shifts in CGN establishment risk across the CONUS (Rossi et al. 2026).
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the entire 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: 4. Emerald ash borer (Agrilus planipennis)
text:
4A. Introduction
The emerald ash borer (EAB), Agrilus planipennis Fairmaire (Coleoptera: Buprestidae), is a flat-headed, wood-boring beetle native to eastern Asia that relies almost exclusively on ash trees (Fraxinus species) to complete its life cycle (Poland et al. 2015, USDA-APHIS 2025). It was first detected in North America in 2002 in Michigan and Ontario, although it likely arrived in Michigan during the early to mid-1990s (Siegert et al. 2014). EAB is now present in 37 U.S. states and six Canadian provinces (EPPO 2025, USDA-APHIS 2025). Adult beetles lay eggs in bark crevices, and upon hatching, larvae burrow into the tree to feed on the inner phloem, outer xylem, and cambium. They overwinter as larvae or pre-pupae within characteristic serpentine galleries beneath the bark (Tluczek et al. 2011, Poland et al. 2015). This feeding disrupts the tree’s ability to transport water and nutrients, typically leading to tree death within several years (Knight et al. 2013). EAB’s cryptic nature, in which all life stages except for the adult beetle are inside of trees, makes early detection of this pest extremely difficult (Haack et al. 2002, USDA-APHIS 2025).
Previous modeling studies indicated broad climatic suitability for EAB across North America that overlapped with the ranges of native Fraxinus species (DeSantis et al. 2013, Sobek-Swant et al. 2012, Liang & Fei 2014, , Barker et al. 2023). All North American ash species are vulnerable to EAB, though blue ash (F. quadrangulata Michaux) appears to be less preferred (Poland et al. 2015). In its native range, the beetle primarily infests stressed or weakened trees, whereas in North America it readily attacks both healthy and stressed individuals, with stressed trees often supporting higher beetle densities (Poland and McCullough 2006, Tluczek et al. 2011). Other members of the olive family, such as white fringetree (Chionanthus virginicus L.) and olive (Olea europaea L.), may also serve as hosts, though survival rates on these species appear to be lower (Rutledge and Arango-Velez 2017, Peterson and Cipollini 2020). The economic impact of EAB in the United States has reached billions of dollars, and the widespread loss of ash trees has led to reduced biodiversity and the degradation of important ecosystem services (Kovacs et al. 2010, Aukema et al. 2011, Schrader et al. 2021).
A model for EAB developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The full set of model parameters for EAB, including developmental temperature thresholds, degree-day requirements for individual life stages, and climate stress thresholds and limits, are available at USPest.org (Barker et al. 2023).

title: 4. Emerald ash borer (Agrilus planipennis)
text:
4C. Discussion
Predicted EAB phenology generally shifted toward earlier seasonal events, with the strongest and most spatially extensive trends occurring over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Predicted adult emergence and egg hatch occurred progressively earlier across portions of the East during both study periods, at rates of approximately 0.01–0.9 days per year. Because EAB is widely established across much of this region, these shifts have practical implications for monitoring and management. Pest managers may need to adjust the timing of seasonal activities to maintain their effectiveness. For example, traps targeting adult beetles may need to be deployed earlier in spring to improve early detection of new infestations, while release schedules for biological control agents, including the larval parasitoids Spathius agrili and S. galinae, may need to be adjusted to account for changes in host availability.
In contrast, significant trends toward later adult emergence and egg hatch occurred in parts of the Intermountain West during 2001–2025. These localized patterns may reflect regional differences in temperature trends and seasonal warming, which have not been spatially or seasonally uniform across the United States (NCEI 2021). However, further analysis of temperature trends during the study period is needed to determine whether these differences explain the predicted delays.
Trends in EAB’s phenology should be interpreted in light of some current limitations of the phenology model. First, the model predicts adult emergence solely from degree-day accumulation and does not account for the chilling requirements of overwintering J-larvae, which must receive sufficient winter chilling to terminate obligatory diapause before metamorphosis can begin (Duan et al. 2021, Duan et al. 2026). Because warmer chilling temperatures may delay adult emergence (Duan et al. 2026), the model may overestimate advances in emergence in warmer regions of the United States, including the South. Second, the model assumes a univoltine life cycle, whereas EAB can exhibit a semivoltine life cycle in cooler regions, overwintering as early instars and requiring a second summer of feeding before reaching the J-larval stage (Jones et al. 2019, Bohannon et al. 2022). This extended development may alter the timing and distribution of adult emergence relative to model predictions. Incorporating chilling requirements and regional variation in voltinism could therefore improve the accuracy of predicted phenological trends and their application to monitoring and biological control.
The limited changes in predicted climatic suitability across both time periods indicate that trends in cold and heat stress have not produced broad changes in predicted EAB establishment potential across the CONUS. Although decreasing cold stress across portions of the Upper Midwest could potentially enhance overwintering survival in EAB, it did not substantially increase predicted establishment potential in these regions. Conversely, increasing heat stress in the Southwest may constrain establishment in already warm regions, particularly where it overlaps with the ranges of native Fraxinus species. The lack of substantial increases in predicted suitability in the Upper Midwest is consistent with previous findings that only sufficiently extreme cold, such as that experienced in parts of northern Canada, is likely to limit EAB establishment through overwintering mortality (Venette et al. 2014, Barker et al. 2023). From a management perspective, these findings support continuing EAB surveillance across the CONUS rather than substantially narrowing surveillance efforts based on the observed trends in climatic suitability.
Our findings were broadly consistent with Barker et al. (2023), who reported geographically restricted trends toward earlier predicted first adult emergence of EAB over 2002–2021, including in parts of the Southeast, New England, and Upper Midwest. Our analysis also identified significant trends toward later adult emergence in parts of the interior West over 2001–2025. Both studies identified isolated areas of decreasing climatic suitability in the southwestern United States, consistent with increasing heat stress. Differences between the studies may partly reflect methodological differences, particularly our use of pre-whitening to account for temporal autocorrelation in the Mann–Kendall analysis. Pre-whitening reduces temporal autocorrelation to better satisfy the test’s assumption of independence among observations and can affect the magnitude and spatial extent of statistically significant trends (Kulkarni and von Storch 1995).
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the entire 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: 5. Egyptian cottonworm (Spodoptera littoralis)
text:
5A. Introduction
The Egyptian cottonworm (ECW), Spodoptera littoralis Boisduval (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae), is a highly destructive and polyphagous moth distributed across southern Europe, the Mediterranean Basin, the Middle East, Africa, China, and India (EPPO 2025). With a host range spanning more than 80 plant species in over 40 families, it is a major pest of crops such as cotton, maize, potato, sugarcane, soybeans, vegetables, and wheat (CABI 2022). The larval stage, which consists of six instars, causes significant damage through extensive defoliation, as well as by attacking growing points and mining or cutting stems (Baker and Miller 1974, EFSA 2015, CABI 2022). Although ECW is not established in the United States, it has been intercepted multiple times at United States ports of entry (Ellis 2004).
A model for ECW developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The full set of model parameters for EDW, including developmental temperature thresholds, degree-day requirements for individual life stages, and climate stress thresholds and limits, are available at USPest.org (Barker and Coop 2021).

title: 5. Egyptian cottonworm (Spodoptera littoralis)
text:
5B. Results

i. Phenology

Entire period: 1981–2025
Trends in predicted first adult emergence and egg hatch for ECW over the 44-year period (1981–2025) were predominantly negative, indicating that both phenological events shifted earlier over time (Figure 1, Figure 2). Earlier phenology was predicted across much of the East and South, as well as higher-elevation areas of the West. Statistically significant trends were more spatially restricted, occurring primarily in portions of the East and scattered areas of the Intermountain West. Within these regions, predicted adult emergence and egg hatch shifted earlier by approximately 0.01–0.6 days per year, with some of the largest shifts occurring at higher elevations in the Intermountain West. Trends toward later phenology occurred in a some isolated areas of the West but most were not statistically significant.

Recent period: 2001–2025
Trends in predictions of first adult emergence and egg hatch for ECW over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025) were partially consistent with those observed over the 1981–2025 period. Significant trends towards earlier phenology were similar in magnitude but less spatially extensive, occurring predominantly in parts of the East and Upper Midwest (Figure 3, Figure 4). In contrast, areas exhibiting trends toward later phenological events were somewhat larger and more spatially extensive across the West.

ii. Climatic suitability

Entire period: 1981–2025
Over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025), predicted cold stress for ECW decreased across broad portions of the CONUS, with the strongest changes occurring in the Northeast, Upper Midwest, and Intermountain West (Figure 5). However, trends across the Midwest and South were generally smaller and mostly nonsignificant. Predicted heat stress increased across much of the West and Great Plains, although significant trends were concentrated primarily in the West (Figure 6). When annual accumulated stress units exceed limits specified in DDRP models, climatic suitability may change. However, changes in stress units for ECW did not correspond to widespread shifts in suitability; only a few small areas in California showed significant decreases in predicted suitability (Figure 7).

Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.

Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.

Positive changes (warmer colors) indicate an increased likelihood of establishment, whereas negative changes (cooler colors) indicate a decreased likelihood of establishment.







Recent period: 2001–2025
Many areas that exhibited significant decreases in cold stress for ECW over 1981–2025 no longer showed significant trends during the recent period. These areas were concentrated in scattered patches across the East and South and at higher elevations in the West (Figure 8). Significant increases in predicted cold stress occurred in a few small, isolated areas of the West. Significant increases in heat stress were concentrated in the South, particularly Texas, whereas parts of California showed significant decreases (Figure 9). As in the 1981–2025 analysis, changes in cold and heat stress produced very few significant changes in climatic suitability (Figure 10).

Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.

Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.

title: 5. Egyptian cottonworm (Spodoptera littoralis)
text:
5C. Discussion
Although ECW is not established in the CONUS, understanding predicted changes in phenology can inform surveillance planning. In areas exhibiting significant trends toward earlier phenology, predicted dates shifted earlier by approximately 0.01–0.6 days per year, suggesting that surveillance materials may need to be deployed earlier in the season. Surveillance may be particularly important where these trends overlap with major host production areas, including extensive commercial cotton acreage and intensive fruit and vegetable production across the South and along the West Coast (Sullivan 2014. However, considering trends in more northern areas is also important because migratory moths may be capable of periodic spread into northern regions later in the season (EFSA PLH).
Earlier adult emergence and egg hatch could potentially allow ECW to complete more generations per year, increasing pest pressure and associated crop damage. ECW lacks a true winter diapause and can complete multiple generations under warm conditions (Yathom 1971, Ellis 2004, Miller 1977, Barker and Coop 2021). ECW may complete 3–9 generations depending on climate and host plant (Ellis 2004), with 1–11 generations predicted in environmentally suitable areas in the CONUS (Barker and Coop 2021). Photoperiod may also influence ECW’s response to temperature across different latitudes (Hegazi et al. 2021). A laboratory study revealed interactive effects of temperature and photoperiod on ECW development, with longer photoperiods slowing larval development rates and reducing the number of larval instars (Hegazi et al. 2021). Its development rate may also vary across host plant species (Salama et al. 1971, Shoman et al. 2025). Higher temperatures could increase ECW reproductive rates and affect insecticide effectiveness (Massot et al. 2021).
The climate-stress trend maps showed broad changes in both cold and heat stress, but these changes did not translate into statistically significant shifts in predicted climatic suitability for ECW in only a few isolated areas of California (Death Valley). The contrast between widespread climate-stress trends and limited suitability changes suggests that the modeled climatic limits remain sufficiently broad that changes in individual stress variables do not necessarily alter establishment potential. Previous modeling studies reported suitable environments for ECW throughout the South and Midwest, as well as along the West Coast, whereas cold temperatures would likely exclude the pest from colder regions, including the Intermountain West and latitudes north of ca. 41° N in the East (Barker and Coop 2021, ElShahed et al. 2023).
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the entire 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: 6. False codling moth (Thaumatotibia leucotreta)
text:
6A. Introduction
Native to sub-Saharan Africa, the false codling moth (FCM), Thaumatotibia leucotreta Meyrick (Lepidoptera: Tortricidae), is a highly polyphagous pest distributed throughout much of Africa and parts of the Middle East, including Israel (Carstens and Moore 2020). Economically important hosts include avocado, Citrus spp., corn, cotton, eggplant, grapes, stone fruits, peppers, and cut roses (EPPO 2025). FCM undergoes five larval instars, during which larvae bore into and feed within plant tissues, particularly fruit, causing direct damage before exiting the host to form cocoons in the soil (NAPPFAST 2003, Gilligan et al. 2011). In 2008, a single adult male was discovered in Ventura County, California, representing the first domestic detection of FCM, extensive subsequent trapping failed to detect additional individuals, and the introduction was successfully eradicated (Gilligan et al. 2011). Although FCM is not established in the United States, it has been repeatedly intercepted at United States ports of entry in both cargo and passenger baggage (Stibick 2006). If established in the United States, FCM could cause substantial economic losses, potentially reaching billions of dollars (Venette et al. 2003, Stibick 2006).
A model for FCM developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the CONUS at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The full set of model parameters for FCM, including developmental temperature thresholds, degree-day requirements for individual life stages, and climate stress thresholds and limits, are available at USPest.org (Barker and Coop 2019).

title: 6. False codling moth (Thaumatotibia leucotreta)
text:
6B. Results

i. Phenology

Entire period: 1981–2025
Trends in predicted first adult emergence and egg hatch for FCM over the 44-year period (1981–2025) were predominantly negative, indicating that both phenological events shifted earlier over time (Figure 1, Figure 2). Earlier phenology was predicted across much of the eastern, south-central, and western United States. Statistically significant trends were more spatially restricted, occurring primarily in portions of the eastern and southwestern United States and scattered areas of the Intermountain West. Within these regions, predicted adult emergence and egg hatch shifted earlier by approximately 0.01–0.6 days per year, with some of the largest shifts occurring in more southern regions. Trends toward later phenology occurred in a some isolated areas of the Great Plains and Intermountain West but most were not statistically significant.








Figure 1: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first adult emergence for FCM across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.













Figure 2: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first egg hatch for FCM across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.







Recent period: 2001–2025
Trends in predictions of first adult emergence and egg hatch for FCM over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025) were partially consistent with those observed over the 1981–2025 period. Trends became more spatially heterogeneous, with significantly later predicted events across portions of the central and northern United States and earlier events in parts of the southeastern and western United States (Figure 3, Figure 4). title: 6. False codling moth (Thaumatotibia leucotreta)
text:
6C. Discussion
Although FCM is not established in the CONUS, understanding predicted changes in phenology can inform surveillance planning. In areas exhibiting significant trends toward earlier phenology, predicted dates shifted earlier by approximately 0.01–0.6 days per year, suggesting that surveillance materials may need to be deployed earlier in the season.
FCM can complete 2–10 generations per year, with the number of generations influenced by temperature, food availability and quality, photoperiod, humidity, and latitude (Venette et al. 2003, Gilligan et al. 2011). In environmentally suitable areas of the contiguous United States (CONUS), FCM is predicted to complete 1–9 generations (Barker and Coop 2019). Drought and associated changes in host-plant availability may contribute to variation in FCM developmental rates and host use (Gilligan et al. 2011), while experimental evidence indicates that moisture stress can also affect FCM development and infestation of tomato (Patrick et al. 2021).
Decreases in predicted cold stress across parts of the CONUS, particularly in the southern United States and California, indicate that cold conditions have become less limiting to FCM establishment in these regions. These areas warrant particular attention because California and Texas account for a large proportion of U.S. citrus production and also grow other crops susceptible to FCM, including avocados, peaches, and cotton. Previous assessments have also identified parts of these regions as potentially suitable for FCM establishment. A biome-based risk map identified parts of Florida and the western United States, excluding the Pacific Coast, as suitable for establishment (Venette et al. 2003). Although Mediterranean climates, including California, were previously considered unsuitable for FCM (EPPO 2013), subsequent modeling predicted suitable conditions in California and other parts of the Pacific Coast, as well as portions of the southern United States (Barker and Coop 2019). Together, these findings support continued surveillance in regions where suitable crop hosts coincide with potentially favorable climatic conditions.
Nevertheless, significant increases in predicted heat stress—and corresponding reductions in establishment risk—occurred in the hottest parts of the southwestern United States, primarily in the Sonoran Desert region. These trends suggest that, despite the presence of suitable crop hosts, some areas may be becoming less favorable for FCM establishment. However, climatic tolerance may differ among FCM life stages: although the pest has limited capacity for rapid cold hardening over short periods, larvae can tolerate a broader range of temperatures than adults, whereas adults exhibit a heat-hardening response (Stotter and Terblanche 2009, Terblanche et al. 2017). In addition, FCM establishment may depend on factors beyond temperature, including food availability, photoperiod, humidity, and latitude (get citations). Therefore, climate-stress trends should be interpreted as one component of establishment risk rather than as a definitive measure of establishment potential.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

6A. Introduction
Native to sub-Saharan Africa, the false codling moth (FCM), Thaumatotibia leucotreta Meyrick (Lepidoptera: Tortricidae), is a highly polyphagous pest distributed throughout much of Africa and parts of the Middle East, including Israel (Carstens and Moore 2020). Economically important hosts include avocado, Citrus spp., corn, cotton, eggplant, grapes, stone fruits, peppers, and cut roses (EPPO 2025). FCM undergoes five larval instars, during which larvae bore into and feed within plant tissues, particularly fruit, causing direct damage before exiting the host to form cocoons in the soil (NAPPFAST 2003, Gilligan et al. 2011). In 2008, a single adult male was discovered in Ventura County, California, representing the first domestic detection of FCM, extensive subsequent trapping failed to detect additional individuals, and the introduction was successfully eradicated (Gilligan et al. 2011). Although FCM is not established in the United States, it has been repeatedly intercepted at United States ports of entry in both cargo and passenger baggage (Stibick 2006). If established in the United States, FCM could cause substantial economic losses, potentially reaching billions of dollars (Venette et al. 2003, Stibick 2006).
A model for FCM developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the CONUS at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The full set of model parameters for FCM, including developmental temperature thresholds, degree-day requirements for individual life stages, and climate stress thresholds and limits, are available at USPest.org (Barker and Coop 2019).

title: 7. Japanese beetle (Popillia japonica)
text:
7A. Introduction
Native to Japan, the Japanese beetle (JPB), Popillia japonica Newman (Coleoptera: Scarabaeidae), is a highly polyphagous pest with a host range exceeding 400 plant species, including food crops, fruit trees, turfgrass, and ornamental plant (Fleming 1972, EPPO 2025, Tayeh et al. 2023). Since its initial detection in the United States in 1916 in New Jersey, JPB has spread widely across the eastern and central regions of the country, as well as parts of eastern Canada (Dickerson and Weiss 1918, Fleming 1972, EPPO 2025, Althoff and Rice 2022). Although isolated infestations have been successfully eradicated in several western states, including Nevada and California, the beetle persists in localized areas of the Pacific Northwest, including parts of Colorado, British Columbia, Washington, and Oregon (Althoff and Rice 2022, EPPO 2025, Stoven et al. 2021). Total associated costs of JPB in the United States are estimated at $460 million annually, with $234 million a year spent on control and turf replacement costs (Fleming 1972, USDA-APHIS 2015).
A model for JPB developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The full set of model parameters for JPB, including developmental temperature thresholds, degree-day requirements for individual life stages, and climate stress thresholds and limits, are available at USPest.org (Barker and Coop 2024).

text:
7B. Results

i. Phenology

Entire period: 1981–2025
Predicted adult emergence and egg hatch for JPB shifted significantly earlier across large portions of CONUS over the entire period (1981–2025), including most East Coast states, parts of the southern and midwestern United States, and the Intermountain West (Figure 1, Figure 2). In these regions, predicted adult emergence and egg hatch decreased by approximately 0.01–0.5 days per year, with some of the largest declines occurring at higher elevations in the northeastern and western United States.

Recent period: 2001–2025
Trends in predictions of first adult emergence and egg hatch for JPB over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025) were partially consistent with those observed over the 1981–2025 period. In the eastern United States, significant trends were similar in magnitude but less spatially extensive (Figure 3, Figure 4), occurring mostly in East coast states and certain parts of the northern Midwest. Most trends in the western United States were not were not significant. In contrast to the longer-term trends, some isolated areas of the interior West, primarily in the southern Intermountain West, exhibited significant trends toward later phenological events.

Entire period: 1981–2025
Significant trends in predicted cold stress for JPB over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025) were predominantly negative (Figure 5), indicating a general decrease in cold stress over time. In contrast, significant trends in heat stress were largely positive across portions of the South and West, indicating increasing heat stress (Figure 6). When annual accumulated stress units exceed limits specified in DDRP models, climatic suitability may change. Consistent with these trends, suitability for JPB increased in Minnesota, but decreased in portions of the Southwest (Figure 7). However, these changes were statistically significant only in parts the Southwest and California, suggesting that changes in predicted heat stress may reduce the likelihood of JPB establishment in these areas.

Statistically significant trends in predicted heat and cold stress for JPB during the recent period (2001–2025) were more spatially limited than those observed over the entire period (1981–2025) (Figure 8, Figure 9). Areas with significant increases in heat stress were generally consistent between the two periods, whereas several areas that exhibited significant decreases in cold stress over the entire period, including the Great Lakes region, no longer showed significant trends. Conversely, parts of the Great Plains and Rocky Mountains exhibited significant increases in cold stress during the recent period. Trends in predicted climatic suitability were broadly consistent with those observed over the entire period but were less spatially extensive, with significant decreases in suitability confined to isolated areas of the Southwest and California, where heat stress increased (Figure 10).

title: 7. Japanese beetle (Popillia japonica)
text:
7C. Discussion
Because JPB is widely established across much of the East and Midwest, trends toward earlier predicted adult emergence and egg hatch could have practical implications for monitoring and management. Pest managers may need to adjust the timing of seasonal activities to maintain their effectiveness. For example, traps targeting adult beetles may need to be deployed earlier to improve early detection of new infestations, while insecticide treatments targeting larvae may need to be applied earlier because first- and second-instar larvae are more susceptible to insecticides than older larvae. Similarly, releases of larval parasitoids, such as Tiphia vernalis (Rohwer), may need to be timed to coincide with earlier larval development.
A trend toward earlier phenological events could increase the likelihood of univoltinism in cooler regions. Although JPB is generally univoltine in the United States, semivoltinism has been reported in colder areas, such as New England, where larvae overwinter a second winter as second or third instars in the soil, typically beneath managed turfgrass (Fleming 1972, Vittum 1986). Consistent with field observations, a CLIMEX model predicted univoltinism across most of the beetle’s current North American range, but semivoltinism in the Northeast and along the United States–Canada border (Kistner-Thomas 2019).
Although cold stress declined for JPB in northern and high-elevation regions of the CONUS, these changes did not translate into significant shifts in predicted establishment risk. However, previous research linked JPB occurrence at its expanding range edge in the Midwest and Great Plains to minimum temperatures and long-term weather trends (Kucherov et al. 2025), suggesting that changes in cold stress could influence its distribution over time. Declining cold stress may also reduce the effectiveness of Ovavesicula popilliae, a microsporidian biocontrol agent that increases JPB larval mortality under cold overwintering conditions (Smitley et al. 2026). In contrast, Kucherov et al. (2025) found negative associations between JPB occurrence and maximum temperature, consistent with our finding of significant declines in predicted climatic suitability across the Southwest and California, where heat stress increased over both the entire (1981–2025) and recent (2001–2025) periods. These declines also align with evidence that JPB survival is low under hot, dry conditions ( Fleming 1972, Vittum 1986, Allsopp 1996).
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the entire 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: 8. Japanese pine sawyer beetle (Monochamus alternatus)
text:
8A. Introduction
The Japanese pine sawyer beetle (JPSB), Monochamus alternatus Hope (Coleoptera: Cerambycidae), is a major vector of nematodes that cause pine wilt disease, particularly Bursaphelenchus xylophilus (Vicente et al. 2012, EPPO 2024). Native to East Asia, including mainland China, Taiwan, Laos, Korea, and Japan, JPSB has expanded its range to other parts of Asia, including Vietnam (Kobayashi et al. 1984, Ma et al. 2006, EPPO 2024). Adult beetles acquire and transmit nematodes while feeding on healthy pine trees, with infection disrupting xylem function and causing wilt and, in susceptible trees, death within weeks (Kobayashi et al. 1984, Vicente et al. 2012). Females primarily oviposit in weakened or diseased trees, where larvae develop beneath the bark and in the sapwood, nematodes subsequently associate with newly emerging adults, completing the transmission cycle (Kobayashi et al. 1984, Ma et al. 2006, An et al. 2019). Although B. xylophilus is native to North America and generally causes little damage in its native range, JPSB could also vector other nematode species not currently present in North America (CAPS 2013, An et al. 2019). JPSB primarily attacks conifers, particularly Pinus, Abies, Picea, Larix, and Cedrus, and pine wilt disease has caused extensive tree mortality and substantial economic losses where it has been introduced, particularly in Asia and Europe (Vicente et al. 2012, An et al. 2019).
Areas suitable for JPSB are predicted throughout much of the southern and midwestern United States, whereas cold temperatures may limit establishment in colder regions, including parts of the Intermountain West and Northeast (Song and Xu 2006, Barker and Coop 2020), Gao et al. 2023). Parts of the West Coast, including most of California, were also predicted to be suitable by some models (Song and Xu 2006, Barker and Coop 2020). Within environmentally suitable areas of the contiguous United States, JPSB is predicted to complete at least one generation annually, with up to four generations in the South (Barker and Coop 2020). In colder parts of its native range, JPSB may be univoltine or semivoltine, whereas 2–3 generations can occur annually in warmer regions such as subtropical and tropical China (Togashi 1989, Ma et al. 2006, CAPS 2013). JPSB undergoes winter diapause primarily during the final larval instar, with diapause induction influenced by larval density (Togashi 2021).
A model for Japanese pine sawyer beetle developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 12.2 °C and upper threshold of 35 °C for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the larva is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of −4 °C and 36 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for Japanese pine sawyer beetle, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-jpsb-parameters. Details on model parameterization are available at USPest.org (Barker and Coop 2020).

title: 8. Japanese pine sawyer beetle (Monochamus alternatus)
text:
8C. Discussion
The JPSB results indicate earlier phenology across many regions over the full period, with more limited and heterogeneous changes during 2001–2025. Because JPSB is associated with conifer hosts and its development is temperature dependent, regional shifts in emergence and egg hatch could alter the timing of detection and management activities. The stronger long-term pattern suggests that recent variability may be obscuring some of the longer-term directional signal.
The increase in predicted climatic suitability across portions of the northern United States over the full period is consistent with the concurrent decline in cold stress in those regions. This pattern suggests that warming may reduce cold-related limitations on establishment. During the recent period, increases in cold stress in parts of the northern interior corresponded with weaker suitability changes, illustrating how shorter-term regional climate patterns can alter the establishment signal.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: 9. Light brown apple moth (Epiphyas postvittana)
text:
9A. Introduction
Native to Australia, the light brown apple moth (LBAM), Epiphyas postvittana (Walker) (Lepidoptera: Tortricidae), is an invasive species established in the United States, the United Kingdom, New Zealand, New Caledonia, and the Azores, with additional interceptions reported worldwide (Danthanarayana 1975, EPPO 2024). This highly polyphagous pest has a host range exceeding 500 plant species, although its most significant economic impacts have been observed in apples, pears, and grapes (Brockerhoff et al. 2011). Infestations can create market access challenges due to the risk of transporting live larvae on a wide variety of host plants (Suckling and Brockerhoff 2010). In the United States, its distribution is currently limited to Hawaii, where it was first reported in 1893, and California, where it was confirmed in 2007 and now persists primarily in the San Francisco Bay Area, the Central Coast, and parts of southern California (Zimmerman 1978; Suckling and Brockerhoff 2010; Barker et al. 2020).
Previous modeling studies indicated suitable environmental conditions for LBAM across much of the southeastern United States and along the Pacific coast (Lozier & Mills 2011, He et al. 2012, Barker et al. 2020). Because LBAM does not undergo winter diapause, its distribution and population persistence are likely constrained in colder regions by minimum winter temperatures (Bürgi and Mills 2010). Cold tolerance varies among larval instars, with reported lower lethal temperatures ranging from –10.5 °C to –0.9 °C (Bürgi and Mills 2010), and associations with certain host plants may further increase larval cold tolerance and overwintering survival (Morey et al. 2016). In warmer regions, the absence of diapause or other strong seasonal synchronizing cues, such as photoperiod or temperature, allows LBAM to maintain overlapping generations throughout the year (Buergi et al. 2011). Consistent with this life-history strategy, the DDRP model predicted as many as nine generations per year in portions of the contiguous United States in 2018, although field observations in California reported an average of 3.27 generations in San Francisco and 4.58 generations in Santa Cruz (Buergi et al. 2011, Barker et al. 2020). Beyond temperature, population growth may also be influenced by rainfall and relative humidity, with higher growth rates reported under cooler temperatures and moderate moisture conditions (Danthanarayana 1995). Together, these findings indicate that LBAM risk is influenced by multiple interacting environmental factors, including winter temperature, temperature during the growing season, and moisture conditions.
A model for LBAM developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 7.2 °C and upper threshold of 31.1 °C for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the larva is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of 3 °C and 31 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for LBAM, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-lbam-parameters. Details on model parameterization are available at USPest.org (Barker et al. 2020). The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 7.2 °C and an upper developmental threshold of 31.1 °C to all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes that the larva is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies thresholds of 3 °C and 31 °C for cold and heat stress, respectively.

title: 9. Light brown apple moth (Epiphyas postvittana)
text:
9C. Discussion
The LBAM maps show broad changes in predicted phenology over the full period, with many regions experiencing earlier adult emergence and egg hatch. Because LBAM is a multivoltine pest whose development is strongly temperature dependent, earlier seasonal activity could increase the period during which populations can develop and reproduce in environmentally suitable areas. The recent-period maps show that these long-term patterns are not uniform through time, emphasizing the importance of considering both long-term trends and recent climate variability.
The combination of decreasing cold stress and increasing heat stress produced relatively broad changes in predicted climatic suitability over the full period. In northern regions, declining cold stress may reduce a major climatic constraint, whereas increasing heat stress in the warmest regions could offset potential suitability gains. The more limited recent-period suitability changes suggest that establishment potential has been comparatively stable in many regions during the shorter period.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: 10. Oak ambrosia beetle (Platypus quercivorus)
text:
10A. Introduction
The oak ambrosia beetle (OAB), Platypus quercivorus Murayama (Coleoptera: Platypodidae), is a destructive forest pest distributed across India, Indonesia, Japan, and Papua New Guinea (Davis et al. 2005; USDA-APHIS 2011; EPPO 2020). The beetle vectors its symbiotic fungal pathogen, Raffaelea quercivora Kubono & Shin-Ito, which causes Japanese oak wilt disease (JOW) by disrupting tracheary function and can kill both healthy and stressed trees (Kubono and Ito 2002; Kamata et al. 2002; Davis et al. 2005; Kobayashi and Ueda 2005). Suitable host plants for reproduction include species of Quercus as well as other members of the Fagaceae, including chestnut (Castanea spp.), chinquapin (Castanopsis spp.), and stone oaks (Lithocarpus spp.), although OAB may also attack non-host tree species near areas experiencing mass infestation (Davis et al. 2005). The beetle–fungus complex has caused extensive oak mortality in Japan, where OAB preferentially attacks larger trees with higher water content, making abandoned oak coppice forests particularly vulnerable to infestation (Kobayashi and Ueda 2005; Nakajima 2019; EPPO 2020). If introduced to the United States, OAB and JOW could pose substantial economic, environmental, and social risks because of the potential for mortality of susceptible oak and other Fagaceae species. Although R. quercivora has only been reported from Japan, the distribution of OAB across multiple countries in Asia and Oceania highlights the potential for movement of the beetle through international trade and other pathways (Davis et al. 2005; USDA-APHIS 2011; EPPO 2020).
Several studies have predicted suitable conditions for OAB across much of the United States, although the predicted range varies among studies (USDA-APHIS 2011; Barker and Coop 2020; Takeuchi et al. 2023). Suitable conditions have been predicted across most of the country, including much of the Pacific Coast, Puerto Rico, and Hawaii, with the northern Midwest generally representing areas of lower suitability (USDA-APHIS 2011; Barker and Coop 2020; Takeuchi et al. 2023). Areas with abundant oak resources would therefore be expected to face the greatest risk of establishment and impact. OAB could potentially complete one to three generations annually in the United States, compared with generally one generation per year in Japan, although a second generation may occasionally occur (Kamata et al. 2002; Barker and Coop 2020; Takeuchi et al. 2023). When development is incomplete before winter, larvae overwinter as fifth instars (Kinuura 1995, Kinuura 2002, USDA-APHIS 2011). OAB is also capable of active flight and exhibits greater flight activity under humid conditions, while warmer temperatures during the rainy season may further increase dispersal activity (EPPO 2020; Kobayashi 2020).
A model for OAB developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 11.1 ºC and upper threshold of 38 ºC for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the larva is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of −10 °C and 38 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for OAB, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-oab-parameters. Details on model parameterization are available at USPest.org (Barker and Coop 2020).

10B. Results

i. Phenology

Entire period: 1981–2025
Over 1981–2025, predicted adult emergence and egg hatch generally shifted earlier across much of the southern and central United States, with later events in portions of the northern interior (Figure 1, Figure 2). Predicted cold stress decreased across broad portions of the northern United States over 1981–2025, while heat stress increased across the Southwest and southern Great Plains (Figure 5, Figure 6). Significant increases in climatic suitability were concentrated in portions of the northern United States, including areas around the Great Lakes and northern Plains (Figure 7).

title: 10. Oak ambrosia beetle (Platypus quercivorus)
text:
10C. Discussion
Predicted phenology for OAB generally shifted earlier over the full period, particularly across the eastern and central United States. These changes could alter the seasonal timing of adult activity and detection in regions where the pest can establish. The reduction in spatial extent during the recent period suggests that shorter-term climate variability has moderated some of the longer-term phenological signal.
The increase in predicted suitability across portions of the northern United States corresponds with decreasing cold stress over the same period, suggesting that cold conditions have become less limiting in these regions. Recent increases in cold stress across parts of the northern interior were accompanied by fewer significant suitability changes, indicating that the establishment signal is sensitive to the period examined.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: 11. Old world bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera)
text:
11A. Introduction
The Old World bollworm (OWBW), Helicoverpa armigera (Hübner) (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae), is a highly polyphagous pest that feeds on agricultural crops from 68 plant families, including chickpea, corn, cotton, tobacco, tomato, potato, and soybean (Cunningham and Zalucki 2014, EPPO 2020). Larvae are the primary damaging life stage of OWBW, as feeding by larvae directly damages vegetative and reproductive plant tissues and can cause substantial yield loss (Rogers and Brier 2010, Cameron et al. 2001). It is widely distributed across much of Europe, Asia, Africa, and Australasia, and began expanding into Central and South America in 2013 (EPPO 2025). In 2015, several specimens were detected in Florida, although populations did not become established (Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services 2015). The species is capable of long-distance migration, traveling up to 2,000 km when assisted by favorable winds (Widmer and Schofield 1983). It has also developed resistance to multiple insecticides and some transgenic crops (EFSA 2014). If established in the United States, OWBW could place crops valued at an estimated $78 billion annually at risk of damage (Kriticos et al. 2015).
Environmental suitability for OWBW is widespread across the United States, with modeling studies predicting suitable conditions across much of the eastern United States and portions of the West (Kriticos et al. 2015, Coop 2018). In the United States, the number of generations per year varies geographically, with up to 10 generations predicted in Florida, while generation numbers are lower in more temperate regions (Coop 2018). Under favorable conditions, generations can be completed in approximately 30 days, and up to 12 generations per year have been reported in tropical regions (EPPO 2020). OWBW is highly fecund, with females producing up to 3,000–4,000 eggs and eggs hatching in as little as three days under optimal conditions (Hardwick 1965, Silva et al. 2018). The species can enter facultative diapause in response to temperature and photoperiod, with diapause incidence increasing with latitude, short-day photoperiods at 20 °C can induce diapause during the early fifth instar, although low temperatures may also induce diapause independently of photoperiod under appropriate conditions (Hackett and Gatehouse 1982, Nibouche 1998, Kurban et al. 2005, Mironidis and Savopoulou-Soultani 2012, Shimizu et al. 2006). Development and population dynamics may also vary among host plant species (Liu et al. 2004, Silva et al. 2018).
A model for OWBW developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 10.6 ºC and upper threshold of 38 ºC for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the pupa is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of −4 °C and 39 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for OWBW, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-owbw-parameters. Details on model parameterization are Online at USPest.org (Coop 2018).
