title: 11. Old world bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera)
text:
11C. Discussion
The OWBW maps indicate widespread regional changes in phenological timing, with earlier adult emergence and egg hatch occurring across many portions of the CONUS over the full period. Because OWBW is highly polyphagous and can have multiple generations in suitable climates, earlier development could increase the period available for population growth and reproduction in regions that remain environmentally suitable.
The decline in cold stress across northern regions and corresponding increases in climatic suitability suggest a potential reduction in cold limitation over the long term. Increasing heat stress in the Southwest may counteract this effect at the warm end of the species’ climatic range. The more limited recent-period suitability changes indicate that establishment potential has not changed uniformly during the shorter period.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: 12. Pine-tree lappet moth (Dendrolimus pini)
text:
12A. Introduction
The pine-tree lappet moth, Dendrolimus pini Linnaeus (Lepidoptera: Lasiocampidae) (PTLM), is an economically important pest of pine trees that is native to Europe and Asia (Hardin and Suazo 2012). Its current range includes Europe, Russia, Kazakhstan, Northern China, and Morocco (Hardin and Suazo 2012, EPPO 2024). PTLM’s primary host is the Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris), but it can successfully develop on 17 other species of pine, Douglas fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii), and Eastern hemlock (Tsuga canadensis), and may be able to successfully develop on Pinus spp. outside of its current range (Hardin and Suazo 2012, Łukowski 2021). Surviving affected trees take several years to recover from defoliation and are more susceptible to other forest pests (Hardin and Suazo 2012). If introduced to the United States, PTLM could cause significant damage to forests dominated by pine and monoculture pin plantations, potentially resulting in economic damage to the timber and Christmas tree industries (Hardin and Suazo 2012, Ray et al. 2016).
Climate suitability models indicate that PTLM could establish across much of the contiguous United States, although predictions vary among models, with the most suitable areas generally concentrated in temperate forest regions of the Northeast, Midwest, Appalachia, and Pacific Northwest (Barker and Coop 2020, Hardin and Suazo 2012). In Europe, the species is typically univoltine but may require two or more years to complete its life cycle in cooler regions (Moore and Evans 2016, Sukovata 2019). DDRP predicts one generation per year across much of the western and northern United States, two generations in parts of Appalachia and the Midwest, and three to four generations in portions of the Southeast (Barker and Coop 2020). Host species can affect larval and pupal development rates, and photoperiod regulates diapause and subsequent spring emergence (Hardin and Suazo 2012, Winokur 1991, Łukowski 2021). PTLM outbreaks have also been associated with warmer and drier conditions, which may influence pest development directly or indirectly through effects on the host plant (Lesniak 1976, Hardin and Suazo 2012, Moore and Evans 2016, Hentschel et al. 2018).
A model for PTLM developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 7.2 ºC and upper threshold of 30.0 ºC for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the larva is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of −15 °C and 30 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for PTLM, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-ptlm-parameters. Details on model parameterization are Online at USPest.org (Barker and Coop 2020).

title: 12. Pine-tree lappet moth (Dendrolimus pini)
text:
12C. Discussion
Predicted phenology for PTLM was more spatially heterogeneous than for several of the other species, particularly during the recent period. Earlier egg hatch across broad areas could shift the timing of early-season activity, whereas the contrasting adult-emergence patterns indicate that different stages may respond differently to regional climate trends. Management timing may therefore benefit from considering multiple phenological events rather than relying on a single event.
The full-period increase in predicted suitability across portions of the central and eastern United States coincided with widespread decreases in cold stress and increasing heat stress in warmer regions. The recent-period increase in cold stress across parts of the northern interior may help explain the reduced spatial extent of suitability changes during 2001–2025.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: 13. Spotted lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula)
text:
13A. Introduction
The spotted lanternfly (SLF), Lycorma delicatula (White) (Hemiptera: Fulgoridae), is a highly polyphagous planthopper that feeds on a broad range of agricultural and non-agricultural plants, including grapevines, fruit and nut trees, and ornamental species (Chu 1930, Barringer and Ciafré 2020, EPPO 2025). Adults cause direct damage by feeding on plant sap, while the accumulation of honeydew promotes the growth of sooty mold, which can inhibit photosynthesis and attract additional pests (Dara et al. 2015, Urban and Leach 2023). Native to China, SLF was first detected in the United States in 2014 in Pennsylvania and has since spread to at least 20 eastern states (Urban and Leach 2023, NYSIPM 2025). The widespread presence of its preferred host, tree-of-heaven [Ailanthus altissima (Mill.) Swingle], has facilitated its rapid expansion (Barringer and Ciafré 2020). In suburban and urban environments, SLF can become a significant nuisance, with large aggregations of adults often swarming on trees (Urban and Leach 2023). The species has already caused substantial economic impacts, including estimated annual losses of $8.8 million to New York’s grape industry alone (Pinto et al. 2025).
Modeling studies indicate that SLF has not yet filled its fundamental niche in the contiguous United States (CONUS) under current weather patterns, with suitable conditions extending across much of the Pacific Coast and eastern United States (Jones et al. 2022, Wakie et al. 2019, Barker et al. 2025). The coldest regions of the CONUS, particularly portions of the Midwest and Northeast, may be less suitable for establishment (Wakie et al. 2019, Barker et al. 2025), although urban heat island effects could facilitate establishment in colder areas beyond the currently predicted range (Owen et al. 2024). SLF phenology may also shift in response to changing weather patterns. Analysis of citizen science observations from 2014 to 2022 found earlier adult emergence and later winter die-off as SLF expanded its range in the eastern United States (Owen et al. 2024). However, the effects of temperature, photoperiod, and other environmental factors on egg diapause and developmental rates remain incompletely understood, limiting predictions of how SLF may respond to changing weather patterns (Keena and Nielsen 2021, Calvin et al. 2023). Diapause may buffer populations against weather variability by enhancing overwintering egg survival and accelerating development and fecundity during summer and fall heat waves (Lewkiewicz et al. 2024). SLF is currently considered univoltine, including in warmer regions of China, and whether it can complete multiple generations annually in warmer areas of the United States remains uncertain (Keena and Nielsen 2021, Calvin et al. 2023).
A model for spotted lanternfly developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the CONUS at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 10 °C and upper threshold of 35 °C for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the egg is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of −16 °C and 37 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for spotted lanternfly, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-slf-parameters. Details on model parameterization are available at USPest.org (Barker et al. 2025).

title: 13. Spotted lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula)
text:
13C. Discussion
The SLF maps show a mixed phenological response, with the direction of change varying geographically and between the two periods. The absence of a single dominant spatial direction suggests that the timing of SLF development may respond differently to regional climate trends. Because the species is already capable of substantial spread in North America, localized changes in predicted phenology may be particularly relevant for surveillance timing in newly suitable areas.
Although cold and heat stress changed across broad areas, relatively little of that variation translated into significant changes in predicted climatic suitability. The long-term reduction in cold stress across northern regions could reduce one climatic constraint on establishment, but recent increases in cold stress in portions of the northern interior may have moderated this trend.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: 14. Common or Cotton cutworm (Spodoptera litura)
text:
14A. Introduction
The common or cotton cutworm (SLI), Spodoptera litura (Fabricius, 1775) (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae), is a highly polyphagous pest that feeds on at least 120 plant species, including economically important crops such as corn, cotton, groundnut, potato, soybean, sweet potato, tea, tobacco, and a wide range of vegetables (Venette et al. 2003, Sullivan 2007, Bragard et al. 2019, EPPO 2023). Females lay eggs on host plants, and within a few days, emerging larvae begin feeding on plant tissue, causing extensive damage that can lead to stunted growth and reduced marketability (Sullivan 2007). Native to Southeast Asia, SLI is now distributed across Australia, Oceania, several African islands, Hawaii, and other regions of Asia (Bragard et al. 2019, EPPO 2023). The pest has been present in Hawaii since 1964 and has been intercepted hundreds of times at United States ports of entry, primarily through cargo and passenger baggage (Venette et al. 2003, Sullivan 2007). The species has developed resistance to numerous insecticides and transgenic Bt cotton and is capable of long-distance migration, potentially aided by typhoons (Tu et al. 2010, Fu et al. 2015, Wan et al. 2008, Bragard et al. 2019, Murata et al. 1998). Severe defoliation caused by larval feeding has led to significant crop damage and economic losses in affected regions (Murata et al. 1998, Prasad et al. 2013, Bragard et al. 2019, Maharjan et al. 2023).
Potentially environmentally suitable areas for establishment for SLI in the contiguous United States (CONUS) include much of the southeastern United States and along the Pacific Coast (Coop 2018). If introduced to the United States, SLI could potentially overwinter in protected environments such as greenhouses or establish northern migratory populations (Bragard et al. 2019). Development and fecundity are strongly influenced by temperature, humidity, and host plant quality (Garad et al. 1985, EPPO 2023, Maharjan et al. 2023, Fu et al. 2025). SLI does not undergo diapause and therefore cannot survive winter conditions in areas north of approximately 30°N in China, where it instead establishes seasonal migratory populations (Fand et al. 2015, Fu et al. 2015, Bragard et al. 2019, EPPO 2023). SLI completes 3-12 generations in tropical regions versus three generations in colder parts of its distribution, including northern China (EPPO 2023). Consistent with its high reproductive potential under warm conditions, a DDRP model predicted one to ten possible generations annually in the conterminous United States, with four to six generations predicted across much of the Southeast and California (Coop 2018). SLI may also respond to changing temperatures through shifts in its geographic distribution and population growth, although warming could reduce suitability in some areas if temperatures exceed optimal conditions for development (Fand et al. 2015, Fu et al. 2025).
A model for SLI was developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the CONUS at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 10.6 ºC and upper threshold of 40 ºC for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the pupa is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of −3 °C and 44 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for SLI, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-sli-parameters. Details on model parameterization are available at USPest.org (Coop 2018).

title: 14. Common or Cotton cutworm (Spodoptera litura)
text:
14C. Discussion
The SLI maps indicate that phenological trends vary by event and region, with no single directional pattern dominating the CONUS. This variability suggests that changes in one developmental event should not necessarily be assumed to represent changes in all stages. Where significant phenological shifts occur, monitoring and management schedules may need to be adjusted regionally.
Despite substantial long-term declines in predicted cold stress across northern regions, the climatic-suitability maps showed little significant change. The limited heat-stress signal further suggests that climatic conditions remain broadly within the modeled suitability range across most of the CONUS, at least with respect to the stress thresholds represented by the model.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: 15. Silver Y moth (Autographa gamma)
text:
15A. Introduction
Widespread across Europe, northern Africa, and Asia, the silver Y moth (SLYM), Autographa gamma Linnaeus (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae), is a highly polyphagous defoliator of cereals, Brassica spp., legumes, tobacco, and a wide range of fruit and vegetable crops, with particularly significant impacts on sugar beet (Maceljski and Balarin 1972, Venette et al. 2003, Sullivan and Molet 2007, EPPO 2019, Carneiro 2022). Adults undertake annual migrations to northern breeding regions across Eurasia to avoid the hot, dry conditions of Mediterranean overwintering areas (Honěk et al. 2002, Chapman et al. 2012, Chapman et al. 2015, Saulich et al. 2017, Becher and Revadi 2020). Population outbreaks in these breeding regions occur sporadically and are often associated with periods of unusually wet weather (Maceljski and Balarin 1974, Carneiro 2022). The species is considered a high-risk invasive agricultural pest for the United States, with the potential to damage more than 200 plant species, including lettuce, cabbage, and grape (Sullivan and Molet 2014). It has been intercepted hundreds of times at United States ports of entry on approximately 130 plant taxa and is considered to have a high likelihood of establishment if introduced (Sullivan and Molet 2014).
Potentially suitable environmental conditions for SLYM occur across much of the United States, although winter conditions may prevent long-term persistence across much of the northern United States, where annual migration from southern source populations could allow temporary establishment during the growing season (Barker and Coop 2020, PPQ 2025). In Eurasia, populations generally complete one to four generations per year, with voltinism increasing toward lower latitudes (Saulich et al. 2017, Carneiro 2022). Similarly, SLYM is predicted to complete one to five generations annually in the contiguous United States (CONUS), with the highest voltinism occurring in the Southeast, Southwest, and California (Barker and Coop 2020, PPQ 2025). Hot, dry conditions may also limit populations, with increased drying in the Mediterranean region potentially reducing northward migration and consequently affecting annual population size and generation number (Ellis 2016).
A model for SLYM developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the CONUS at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 8.9 ºC and upper threshold of 35.0 ºC for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the larva is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of −1 °C and 38 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for SLYM, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-slym-parameters. Details on model parameterization are available at USPest.org (Barker and Coop 2020).

15B. Results

i. Phenology

Entire period: 1981–2025
Over 1981–2025, predicted egg hatch and adult emergence generally showed earlier trends across portions of the western and central United States, with later events in portions of the northern and eastern interior (Figure 1, Figure 2). Significant changes were concentrated in scattered areas, particularly in the central and eastern United States.

Figure 2: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first egg hatch for SLYM across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.







Recent period: 2001–2025
During 2001–2025, earlier predicted egg hatch and adult emergence remained evident across portions of the West and central United States, while later events occurred in parts of the northern and eastern United States (Figure 3, Figure 4). Significant changes were spatially limited.

ii. Climatic suitability

Entire period: 1981–2025
Predicted cold stress decreased broadly across the northern United States over 1981–2025, while heat stress increased in the western and southern United States (Figure 5, Figure 6). Changes in predicted climatic suitability were extremely limited, with little significant change across the CONUS (Figure 7).








Figure 5: Changes (units/year) in predicted cold stress for SLYM across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.

Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 7: Changes in predicted climatic suitability for SLYM across the CONUS over the 44-year period (1981–2025). Suitability is defined as areas not excluded by climate stress. Positive changes (warmer colors) indicate an increased likelihood of establishment, whereas negative changes (cooler colors) indicate a decreased likelihood of establishment.

During 2001–2025, cold-stress changes became more mixed, with increases across portions of the northern and central interior (Figure 8). title: 15. Silver Y moth (Autographa gamma)
text:
15C. Discussion
Predicted phenology for SLYM showed regional changes in timing but relatively limited changes in climatic suitability. Earlier events in portions of the West and central United States could shift seasonal activity, while contrasting trends in northern and eastern areas indicate that the response is geographically heterogeneous. The recent-period maps also show that shorter-term climate patterns can differ from the longer-term signal.
The broad decline in cold stress over the full period did not produce a corresponding broad increase in predicted climatic suitability. This suggests that SLYM is not strongly constrained by the modeled cold-stress threshold across most of the CONUS. Increasing heat stress in the Southwest likewise produced little measurable change in overall suitability.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: 16. Small tomato borer (Neoleucinodes elegantalis)
text:
16A. Introduction
The small tomato borer (STB), Neoleucinodes elegantalis (Guenée) (Lepidoptera: Pyralidae), is an oligophagous pest of Solanum species, including tomato, eggplant, red and green pepper, lulo (naranjilla), and wild Solanum spp. (Molet 2012, OEPP/EPPO 2015). Native to South America, it has expanded its range into Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean (Molet 2012, OEPP/EPPO 2015, Díaz-Montilla 2013a). The species occupies a wide range of climatic conditions in South America, although its distribution varies depending on host plant availability and altitude (Díaz Montilla 2013b). Larvae develop through five instars, with the third through fifth instars responsible for the majority of fruit damage, and development rates that may vary by host plant (Serrano Plaza et al. 1992, Díaz-Montilla 2013a). Infestations can result in severe economic losses, with reported yield reductions in South American tomato crops ranging from 45% to 90% (Díaz Montilla and Kondo 2024). If introduced to the United States, regions with high levels of tomato and pepper production would be particularly vulnerable (Molet 2012, USDA-APHIS-PPQ 2024). In addition, STB poses a significant barrier to the export of solanaceous crops from South America to the United States and the European Union (Díaz-Montilla 2013a, Díaz-Montilla 2013b). The pest has been intercepted hundreds of times at United States ports of entry, with most interceptions originating from Brazil (Molet 2012).
Potentially suitable environmental conditions for STB occur in western portions of the Pacific states, the Southeast, and parts of the southern Northeast, although colder conditions limit suitability across much of the northern United States (Barker et al. 2020). In its native range, increases in temperature and precipitation appear to favor STB populations, while arid conditions can limit its distribution, suggesting that moisture availability may influence STB distribution and climatic suitability in the contiguous United States (CONUS; Silva et al. 2020, da Silva et al. 2018). Annual voltinism also varies substantially with climate, with models predicting 2–11 generations per year in Colombia and 5–10 generations in Brazil (de Moraes and Foerster 2015, dos Santos and Marchioro 2021). STB does not appear to have a diapause or distinct overwintering stage and can produce continuous, overlapping generations, with voltinism generally increasing toward warmer, lower-latitude regions (Serrano Plaza et al. 1992, Moraes and Foerster 2015, Barker et al. 2020). In CONUS, annual voltinism is predicted to range from one to two generations in colder parts of the Pacific Northwest to seven to nine generations in coastal areas of the Southeast, with three to six generations across much of the remainder of the CONUS (Barker et al. 2020).
A model for tomato fruit borer developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the CONUS at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 8.89 °C and upper threshold of 30 °C for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the adult is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of 6 °C and 32 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for tomato fruit borer, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-stb-parameters. Details on model parameterization are available at USPest.org (Barker et al. 2020).

title: 16. Small tomato borer (Neoleucinodes elegantalis)
text:
16C. Discussion
The STB results show a clear difference between the long-term and recent phenological patterns. Earlier emergence and egg hatch were common over 1981–2025, whereas later events became more prominent in the recent period across portions of the northern and central United States. This contrast suggests that recent regional climate variability has substantially influenced the short-term phenological signal and should be considered when interpreting current management timing.
The increase in predicted suitability across northern and central regions over the full period coincided with declining cold stress, suggesting that warming has reduced a temperature-related limitation in those areas. The recent increase in cold stress and corresponding reduction in suitability changes indicate that this long-term expansion signal is less evident during 2001–2025.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: 17. Sunn Pest (Eurygaster integriceps)
text:
17A. Introduction
The Sunn pest (SUNP), Eurygaster integriceps Puton, 1881 (Hemiptera: Scutelleridae), is a serious and economically important pest of wheat, barley, oats, rye, and sorghum. Its geographic range spans latitudes 25° to 55° N across Eurasia, including much of Eastern Europe, West Asia, Central Asia, and North Africa (Paulian and Popov 1980, Critchley 1998, Mackesy and Moylett 2018, EPPO 2021). Both larvae and adults damage host plants by causing plant death, arresting grain development, or degrading the gluten content of surviving wheat kernels (Paulian and Popov 1980, Critchley 1998). As a result, flour produced from infested grain yields bread of poor quality and reduced digestibility (Paulian and Popov 1980). In the absence of effective control measures, infestations can lead to complete crop loss (Kivan and Kilic 2005). If introduced to the United States, SUNP could cause substantial economic damage to wheat and barley production, which were valued at $7.9 billion and $685 million, respectively, in 2017 (USDA-NASS 2019). Areas at most risk for establishment of SUNP based on host presence are in the Midwestern United States, the Columbia River valley, and the lower Mississippi River valley (Macksey and Moylett 2018).
SUNP is a univoltine pest with two major periods in its annual life cycle (Davari and Parker 2018). Adults spend late summer through winter in aestivation and overwintering sites, where they undergo obligatory diapause and remain largely inactive until spring temperatures reach approximately 10–14 °C, triggering emergence and migration to cereal fields for reproduction (Banks et al. 1961, Critchley 1998, Parker et al. 2011, Islamoglu 2022). Following development through five nymphal instars and the subsequent adult emergence, adults migrate approximately 10–20 km to hillside aestivation and overwintering sites, which occur at higher elevations under bushes in the southern part of the range and in deciduous Quercus forests in the northern part (Paulian and Popov 1980, Critchley 1998, Davari and Parker 2018). This seasonal movement between agricultural and non-crop habitats complicates management and requires appropriately timed monitoring and control (Critchley 1998, Davari and Parker 2018), while regional geographic features that influence temperature can affect the timing and direction of migration (Parker et al. 2011, Islamoglu 2022). Potentially suitable environmental conditions for SUNP occur across most of the contiguous United States (CONUS), although mountainous and higher-latitude regions of the West may be unsuitable for development because of insufficient thermal accumulation (Aljaryian et al. 2016, Barker and Coop 2020). Nevertheless, the species’ migratory behavior could allow adults to move between suitable cereal-growing areas and nearby seasonal aestivation or overwintering sites, potentially facilitating persistence where seasonal conditions limit activity.
A model for SUNP developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the CONUS at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 12.2 °C and upper threshold of 36 °C for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the adults is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of −30 °C and 40 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for SUNP, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-sunp-parameters. Details on model parameterization are available at USPest.org (Barker and Coop 2020).

title: 17. Sunn Pest (Eurygaster integriceps)
text:
17B. Results

i. Phenology

Entire period: 1981–2025
Over 1981–2025, predicted adult emergence and egg hatch generally shifted earlier across much of the southern and central United States, with later events in portions of the northern interior (Figure 1, Figure 2). Significant changes occurred primarily in the eastern and central United States, with additional localized changes elsewhere.

Recent period: 2001–2025
During 2001–2025, earlier predicted phenology remained evident across much of the West and central United States, while later events occurred in portions of the northern and eastern interior (Figure 3, Figure 4). Significant changes were spatially limited.

Figure 4: Changes (days/year) in predicted dates of first egg hatch for SUNP across the CONUS over the recent 24-year period (2001–2025). Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant.








ii. Climatic suitability

Entire period: 1981–2025
Predicted cold stress decreased across portions of the northern United States over 1981–2025, especially in the northern Plains and Great Lakes, while heat stress increased in the Southwest and southern Great Plains (Figure 5, Figure 6). Climatic suitability increased significantly in portions of the northern Plains and Great Lakes (Figure 7).

Maps show (A) all changes and (B) statistically significant changes (P < 0.1); areas shown in gray are not statistically significant. Areas shown as 0 in (B) had significant trends but very small changes.













Figure 6: Changes (units/year) in predicted heat stress for SUNP across the CONUS over the entire 44-year period (1981–2025). Positive changes (warmer colors) indicate an increased likelihood of establishment, whereas negative changes (cooler colors) indicate a decreased likelihood of establishment.

Heat stress continued to increase in the Southwest and southern Great Plains (Figure 9). Significant suitability changes were limited during the recent period, with small increases remaining in portions of the northern United States (Figure 10).

title: 17. Sunn Pest (Eurygaster integriceps)
text:
17C. Discussion
The SUNP maps indicate earlier phenological timing over much of the CONUS during the full period, but a weaker and more heterogeneous pattern during the recent period. Because SUNP development and seasonal movement are closely associated with temperature and seasonal conditions, these shifts could alter the timing of movement and activity in regions where the species can establish.
The long-term increase in predicted suitability across portions of the northern Plains and Great Lakes is consistent with declining cold stress in those regions. Recent increases in cold stress across parts of the same broad region correspond with fewer significant suitability changes, suggesting that the establishment signal has become less consistent during the recent period.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.

title: 18. TABS (Phthorimaea absoluta)
text:
18A. Introduction
The tomato leaf miner (TABS), Phthorimaea absoluta (Meyrick) (formerly Tuta absoluta) (Lepidoptera: Gelechiidae), is a highly destructive pest of tomato and other solanaceous crops, native to Peru (Biondi et al. 2018). It is now widely distributed across Central and South America and has invaded much of Europe, Africa, and Asia, reaching as far as South Korea (Biondi et al. 2018, EPPO 2025). In China, the species has demonstrated an exceptionally rapid spread, with a median dispersal rate exceeding 1,000 km per day (Xue et al. 2025). In cooler regions, TABS can persist in protected environments such as greenhouses (Desneux et al. 2010, Gao et al. 2025). Early infestations are difficult to detect, and if left unmanaged, the pest can cause complete crop loss (Desneux et al. 2010, Biondi et al. 2018). Its rapid global expansion has led to increased reliance on synthetic insecticides, with associated environmental and health concerns (Desneux et al. 2011). Climate suitability models indicate that major tomato-producing countries, including the United States, Mexico, and Canada, are at high risk of invasion, which could lead to increased tomato prices (Desneux et al. 2011, Biondi et al. 2018).
Higher temperatures generally promote TABS development and abundance, while moisture availability can also influence its survival and population abundance (Cherif et al. 2019, Tonnang et al. 2015, Sylla et al. 2018, Bacci et al. 2021). Occurrence records from Africa suggest that TABS can persist under relatively hot and dry conditions when host plants are available, although low soil moisture and cold winters may limit survival (Tonnang et al. 2015). In Brazil, low rainfall has been associated with higher pest abundance, whereas reduced abundance during the rainy season in Senegal was attributed primarily to limited host-plant availability, suggesting that relationships between moisture and TABS abundance may depend on host availability (Sylla et al. 2018, Bacci et al. 2021). Multiple species distribution models predict suitable conditions for TABS throughout the southeastern United States and along much of the Pacific Coast (Santana et al. 2019, Barker and Coop 2020, Ponti et al. 2021, Marchioro and Krechemer 2024, Gao et al. 2025, Nitta et al. 2025). TABS is multivoltine, with reported annual generation numbers ranging from 2–5 in Bulgaria and four in Turkey to 10–12 in South America and 13 overlapping generations in Spain, where year-round activity has been reported (Desneux et al. 2010, Mamay and Yanik 2012, Karadjova et al. 2013, Vercher Aznar et al. 2010). In the contiguous United States, estimates of annual voltinism range from 3–9 generations under historical climate conditions, with up to 13 generations predicted under favorable conditions (Barker and Coop 2020, Azrag et al. 2023).
A model for TABS developed for the Degree-Day, establishment Risk, and Phenological event mapping system (DDRP) is operationalized to produce near real-time forecasts for the contiguous United States (CONUS) at https://uspest.org/DDRP. The phenology model applies a lower developmental threshold of 7.8 ºC and upper threshold of 35 ºC for all life stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) and assumes the adult is the overwintering stage. The climatic suitability model applies a lower cold stress threshold and upper heat stress threshold of 2 °C and 37 °C, respectively. The full set of model parameters for TABS, including degree-day requirements for individual life stages and climate stress limits, are presented in ?@tbl-tabs-parameters. Details on model parameterization are available at USPest.org (Barker and Coop 2020).

title: 18. TABS (Phthorimaea absoluta)
text:
18C. Discussion
The TABS results show substantial regional variation in predicted phenological change, with the recent period characterized by later adult emergence and egg hatch in portions of the northern and central United States. In environmentally suitable regions, shifts in phenology could affect the timing and number of generations because TABS is multivoltine and its development is strongly temperature dependent. The maps therefore suggest that surveillance and management timing may need to account for regional differences in seasonal development.
The increase in predicted climatic suitability across portions of the southern and central United States is consistent with the species’ modeled preference for warmer conditions and the long-term reduction in cold stress. At the same time, increasing heat stress in the Southwest could limit suitability in the warmest areas. The more localized recent-period suitability changes suggest that establishment risk has not increased uniformly across the CONUS.
The stronger and more spatially extensive trends in predicted phenology and climate stress over the full 44-year period may reflect both the larger sample size, which can reduce noise and improve detection of directional patterns, and differences in the underlying climate trends between the two time periods. In particular, the recent 24-year period may capture climate variability or regional trends that differ from those observed over the longer 44-year period. Thus, differences between the two periods should be interpreted as reflecting both long-term climate trends and shorter-term regional variability.
